People Are Calling The Day Before Thanksgiving ‘Green Wednesday’—And It’s Becoming A Huge Holiday

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Delish

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Thanksgiving is known for plenty of traditions, from arguing over who makes the best mac and cheese to fighting for the last slice of pie.
  • It has been revealed that if you've ever been at Thanksgiving dinner when a group of cousins suddenly announces they're going for a walk, you probably know what's happening.
  • Enter Green Wednesday, the cannabis industry’s answer to Black Friday.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Thanksgiving is known for plenty of traditions, from arguing over who makes the best mac and cheese to fighting for the last slice of pie. But there’s another tradition that's becoming increasingly popular.

It has been revealed that if you've ever been at Thanksgiving dinner when a group of cousins suddenly announces they're going for a walk, you probably know what's happening. The so-called “cousin walk,” when relatives sneak away to smoke weed, has become such a recognizable holiday ritual that it's now inspiring TikTok videos, memes, and an entire shopping event.

Enter Green Wednesday, the cannabis industry’s answer to Black Friday.

Green Wednesday is the day before Thanksgiving, and it has become one of the year’s biggest shopping days for cannabis retailers. This year, it falls on November 25.

The term has been around since at least 2016, when cannabis delivery company Eaze began using it after noticing a surge in purchases ahead of Thanksgiving.

According to MJBizDaily, cannabis retailers recorded approximately $138.5 million in sales on Green Wednesday in 2025, up from $132.4 million the previous year, based on data from cannabis market intelligence manufacturer BDSA.

While Green Wednesday is often described as the industry’s second-biggest shopping day behind 4/20, some retailers are seeing even stronger results.

Recent findings suggest that according to data RISE Dispensaries shared with Delish, Green Wednesday was its biggest sales day of 2025 and outperformed the notorious cannabis holiday 4/20. The company’s sales were roughly double an average Wednesday, while pre-rolls saw their strongest sales day of the year.

A major part of Green Wednesday’s cultural appeal comes from the infamous cousin walk—the tradition has become a recurring joke across social media, with TikTok customers sharing videos about coordinating their annual walkabout. And, of course, brands are getting involved, too.

As Morning Brew reported, Jif referenced cousin walks in an Instagram promotion last year, while a Taco Bell and Hidden Valley collaboration played on a similar holiday joke. Cannabis brand Dogwalkers is also leaning into the tradition with a Cousin Walk Kit tied to Thanksgiving.

And while Green Wednesday and the cousin walk go hand in hand, cannabis use isn't limited to just the cousins.

A 2026 study from UC San Diego found that approximately 8.9% of Americans ages 65 and older had used cannabis in the previous year. Among those users, 40.5% reported consuming cannabis through food or drinks. Meanwhile, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration found that 22.4% of American adults used cannabis in 2025.

It has been revealed that americans’ drinking habits are changing, too. A 2026 Gallup survey found that just 54% of U.S. adults consume alcohol, down from 62% in 2023. While the figures don't establish that people are replacing alcohol with cannabis, they reflect changing consumption habits. It seems people are increasingly opting out of Blackout Wednesday and opting into Green Wednesday.

The growing conversation around edibles also comes with an important reminder: Cannabis-infused foods and drinks can take longer to produce noticeable effects than inhaled cannabis, and they should always be clearly labeled and kept away from children.

Industry observers note that between the sales numbers, viral cousin-walk jokes, and brands embracing the tradition, Green Wednesday is becoming a recognizable part of the Thanksgiving season. So when someone inevitably asks whether anyone wants to go for a walk after dinner, just know that an entire industry has been preparing for that moment.

Alongside her many talents, one quality I particularly applaud my mom for is her expertise in hosting. She is specifically known for what she dubbed “the emergency dinner party.” This is the kind of soirée that, despite being swiftly organized—perhaps after a long day at work or a busy weekend afternoon—never fails to keep guests entertained and impressed. When it comes to appetizers at an emergency dinner party, the objective is to use limited ingredients, ensure ease of assembly, and deliver bangin’ flavor. For my mom’s famous feta artichoke dip, only three ingredients are absolutely crucial: feta, artichoke hearts, and olive oil. The brine from the canned artichoke hearts allows the feta to melt down in the oven, which in turn coats the artichoke hearts, creating a velvety dip. The best part about this recipe is that it’s completely customizable. My favorite variation includes adding honey, thyme, and an olive topper, which elevates the dip to a whole new level. Serve it with crunchy crostini or pita chips at your next dinner party, and your guests will go crazy.

Tech Report: How Women Weavers Are Preserving Indigenous Amazigh Culture in Morocco

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 14 min read (2792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~14 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that malika Oubzou is sitting on a red and blue handwoven rug on the floor of her childhood home in Tamda Noumercid, a small village near Azilal in Morocco’s Atlas Mountains.
  • Industry observers note that soon enough, more food comes out: a steaming clay pot of tajine maazi (goat tagine) with potatoes and carrots, fresh tomato salad, and fluffy Tafarnout bread, still warm from the clay oven.
  • Malika Oubzou greets her neighbors at the door of her home in Azilal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that malika Oubzou is sitting on a red and blue handwoven rug on the floor of her childhood home in Tamda Noumercid, a small village near Azilal in Morocco’s Atlas Mountains. The 36-year-old weaving artisan is enjoying a glass of milk and a plump, juicy date from a large plate she’s set out for guests—myself among them—when she looks up to see even more people arriving. To accommodate the latest visitors, she finishes her milk, leaves the room, and returns with a low table. Then another. And another after that.

Industry observers note that soon enough, more food comes out: a steaming clay pot of tajine maazi (goat tagine) with potatoes and carrots, fresh tomato salad, and fluffy Tafarnout bread, still warm from the clay oven. Malika shifts the tables around to make room for the additional food, and her brother, Mohammed, rearranges the pillows that line the rug-filled floors of the space. It continues like this for the next couple of hours: A table appears here, a pillow moves there. Food comes in and food goes out. The only thing that stays put? The rugs themselves.

Malika Oubzou greets her neighbors at the door of her home in Azilal. In Morocco, Friday is celebrated as "Couscous Day," a cherished tradition where families gather for a communal lunch, usually after the weekly congregational prayer.

Recent findings suggest that “In a typical rural Moroccan household, everything is mobile except the rugs,” Jihane Lahbibi, the Moroccan co-founder of the Moroccan rug brand Casa Amar, tells me as we dunk our Tafarnout into the tagine juices. “The pillows, tables, mattresses…they are all roving. But the rugs are the constant. Symbolically, they are the pillars. They anchor the room. They are the room.” In fact, as Malika echoes later through a translator, rugs are the most sacred part of the home. “When you welcome guests,” she notes, “the rug is everything.”.

Malika was the first weaver Jihane and her Italian husband Matteo met when they began looking for artisans to make custom rugs for Casa Amar back in 2021. Today, they partner with women in five communities across Morocco to create and source rugs for clients across the world, and were even part of Milan Design Week last year. As interest in Moroccan craftsmanship and design continues to soar, I’ve come to spend some time with a few of the artisans Jihane and Matteo work with to learn more about the Amazigh weaving culture behind the craft.

Sources indicate that this scene with the roving tables is a very good start. It’s impossible to miss the deep significance of rugs in everyday Moroccan life once you experience their starring role in every room, after all. But as the days go by, I realize rugs have taken on even more meaning in recent decades, too: They’ve become a way to keep Amazigh culture alive in the face of modernization.

“Younger generations aren’t making as many rugs these days, so when the older women weavers eventually die, the younger ones won’t know how to make them—and that makes me really, really sad,” Malika tells me after we’ve finished our tagine and have moved on to mint tea and a bowl of grapes for dessert. “So now, when I’m weaving, I think about my culture. I also think about the satisfaction of making something good, and the money I will get from making it. All of those things are notable. But rugs are objects that last, and because they last, they are one of the best ways to preserve the culture.”.

Like most Indigenous traditions around the world, Moroccan rug weaving dates back thousands of years. Amazigh women (also known as Berber) in the Atlas Mountains originally crafted handknotted rugs from local sheep’s wool to protect themselves and their families from the elements: harsh sun during the day, and freezing mountain temperatures at night. Over time, rug weaving morphed into an art form as well, one filled with all sorts of storytelling and symbolism. Some rug patterns represent universal emotions like love and hope, while others are more like talismans, meant to protect against evil and infertility. No matter the pattern, though, the weaving tradition itself has never been written down anywhere. It’s passed down from mother to daughter simply by watching.

Sources indicate that nejma Oubzou prepares freshly harvested dwarf palm by cutting the thorns off and separating the fan-like leaves in order to dry them out. The fibers are used to create woven items such as baskets, mats, and home decor.

It has been revealed that “Amazigh women know how to make rugs the same way many other people around the world know how to make bread…it’s just a part of the culture from a very young age,” Jihane, who grew up in Casablanca, tells me one afternoon as we’re driving through the mountains. “It’s not like someone sits you down on the loom and notes, ‘This is how you do it.’ It’s just that you learn the same way you learn how to walk: No one tells you, you just learn it by seeing.” When she started Casa Amar in 2021 after leaving her job as a business lawyer, she used to ask the artisans she met when, exactly, they learned to weave for the first time. But now she’s come to understand that seeking out that information was always a fool’s errand. “I realize now that it was never so specific,” she reflects. “It was always: They’re around, they see, and they try.”.

That’s exactly what happened with Malika. She wove her first rug at age 15 after years of watching her mom weave, and then watching her weave some more. But that first rug she ultimately created wasn’t just a result of growing up around looms; it was a way for her to care for her own mind. When she was 10, her older brother asked her to drop out of school. Their sister had just gotten married, their parents worked outside the home in agriculture, and he and his younger brother wanted to stay in school—so he decided Malika would be the one to stay home and handle the household chores. Weaving became her creative outlet as a result. “What happened was that after I finished my household work, I had this emptiness that I wanted to fill, and weaving was how I filled it,” she tells me. “I didn’t go to school and I didn’t work, so weaving was how I took care of my brain. I used it to fill a void.”.

Today, Malika continues to weave to fulfill her creative dreams, and to make money by doing so. She works independently in the home, not as part of one of the thousands of weaving cooperatives scattered throughout Morocco. When she’s weaving a custom rug for Casa Amar, she follows the design given to her by their clients. But when she’s weaving just for herself or her family (which is increasingly rare due to her growing amount of paid work), her patterns are instinctive and intuitive, usually based on how she is feeling in the moment. “There’s no particular reasoning behind so many of my designs; it’s just what I like and what my mind tells me to do,” she explains. “It’s a very free process. It’s not like if you have green, you have to put yellow. You can do whatever you want. It’s all in the mind when you’re making a rug for yourself.”.

But aside from earning a living and expressing her creativity, there’s a third reason Malika weaves: a desire to preserve her craft in the face of modernization. This is where things get slightly complicated because, in some ways, the tradition is thriving. As any design aficionado knows, the allure of Moroccan textiles is increasingly global and well-documented, everywhere from Instagram to the pages of this very magazine. According to the international research firm 6W, the Moroccan rug market is projected to reach $485 million in the US by 2032, up from $371 million in 2025.

In a recent development, every step of the wool preparation process is done by hand. After the wool is sheared from the animal, the artisans wash, brush, and spin it into yarn.

Recent findings suggest that upcoming York-based interior designer Sarah Lederman believes this uptick in interest could be a response to, take a guess, AI. “People are craving more handmade items in their homes now because they’re the opposite of uniform,” she says, “and Moroccan rugs bear the mark of the person who made them.” They’re a reminder, in other words, of what it means to be human.

Khadija Rhandouss in the carpet section of the weekly souk in Khmisset. Rhandouss is a local businesswoman who trades in Moroccan rugs. Every Tuesday she attends the weekly souk in Khmisset where all the best rug deals happen before sunrise.

At the same time, there are threats to the longevity of traditional rugmaking. For one thing, as Malika mentioned at multiple points throughout my visit, fewer young women are actually learning the traditional weaving techniques required to make mentioned rugs. The work is time-consuming, after all, and the money isn’t always great. And now that there are more profitable career options available elsewhere, many younger women are choosing to leave their villages in the mountains, making weaving less of an obvious path than it once was.

Nejma Oubzou spins wool into yarn at her home in the Atlas Mountains in Morocco.

That’s not to mention the modern technology that has changed the game even more. In the early 2000s, some Moroccan small producers started to buy machines from China that allowed them to process bad-quality wool (known locally as “dead wool”) to make carpets. While starting a fresh rug used to begin with cutting pure wool from sheep, these machines—which are still used by many today—make it easy to cut out that step entirely. This eliminates a huge and significant part of the process. “A lot of people think that making a carpet is just about weaving on a loom, but actually, making the raw material—i.e., transforming it from sheep to the wool that allows you to start weaving—is just as key,” Ibrahim Noubl, a longtime Moroccan rug dealer, told me in Marrakech at the beginning of my trip. He owns Soufny Art Gallery on the edge of the medina, and often collaborates with the beloved, art-filled hotel El Fenn just a two-minute walk down the road. “In Morocco, we are very sentimental people. We believe in lots of non-material ideas, like the thought that wool is blessed,” he explained. “When blessed wool is inside your home, it will bring you comfort and joy—but all of that disappears when it’s not alive in the first place.”.

Mimouna Fadil attaches the wool to a wooden plank to start a new rug at her home in Khmisset.

Artisans, particularly from the Amazigh communities, hand-dye the wool using traditional techniques, often boiling it with ingredients to create long-lasting, eco-friendly colors. Red wool in Moroccan rug making is traditionally achieved using natural dyes derived from plants, minerals, and insects to produce vibrant, lasting colors. Earthy reds often come from henna or madder root, while brighter shades are created with pomegranate peels or cochineal insects.

With that in mind, vintage rugs are one of the best bets for high-quality wool, Ibrahim advises, because the product has already survived a few decades—so you know the wool is good. (Carpets made from “dead wool” often start to smell after a few years.) But to keep the ancient traditions alive in a competitive marketplace, companies like Casa Amar, Salam Hello, and the ever-popular Beni Rugs also sell newly introduced rugs and put traditional, sustainable craftsmanship front and center. Not only do they use high-grade natural wool (no “dead wool” to be found here), but they also work directly with artisans like Malika, helping provide an income that allows them to continue their traditional and beloved craft.

According to recent reports, nejma Oubzou, mother of Malika, in her bedroom in her home in the Atlas Mountains. Her name means “stars.”.

Industry observers note that many of the artisans even pray before they sit down at the loom because it’s such a sacred act. They start with the Arabic phrase “Bismillah,” which means “in the name of God,” then follow it up with a prayer for peace and serenity during their time on the loom, often including phrases like nsaliw l mensej f salam ou l hna: “We started with peace; may we finish with peace.” After all, as Jihane tells me at various points over the course of our week together, a rug can be both sacred and a source of income. The two are not mutually exclusive. “To buyers, rugs may be just random objects, but people pray before making them, even for people they don’t know,” she states one Friday over Friday couscous, a longtime weekly tradition in Morocco. “I never want to romanticize weaving, because at the end of the day, artisans make the rugs to survive. But both can be true. Just because you have to earn money doesn’t mean you don’t make it respectfully the way your elders did it. It’s something you do with dignity and pride…something to carry the legacy.”.

For the last leg of my Morocco trip, Jihane takes me to Khemisset, a small market town about an hour’s drive inland from the capital Rabat, where she lives with Matteo and their two (adorable) young sons. Khemisset is known for its surrounding countryside—think rolling wheat fields, fragrant eucalyptus trees, and grazing sheep—plus its Amazigh weaving traditions, particularly its regionally specific palm mats. Not many artisans make these mats anymore except those in the Khemisset countryside and a few others scattered throughout the Atlas Mountains, and they are sadly going extinct as a result—so I wanted to see them before it’s too late. Jihane and Matteo are also trying to help preserve the mats by spreading the word to their customers. “It’s simple: If people know about them and buy them, artisans will keep making them,” she tells me in the car on the drive from Rabat.

Industry observers note that unlike handknotted rugs, these palm mats are woven from dried palm leaves (not wool) and embroidered with colorful wool patterns on top. They typically cost much less than wool rugs because the raw material is cheaper, but they’re equally difficult to make—and a bit harder on the hands. The leaves tend to dry out during the day, even after the artisans boil them for softness and place them in sachets. As a result, the six women I meet—all of whom collaborate with Jihane and Matteo—often weave late into the night when it’s cooler, or in the morning before the sun becomes too strong. Despite these challenging conditions, they love what they do and are determined to keep the craft alive. (Not entirely unrelated, they are also determined to stuff me and Jihane with more dates, milk, Tafarnout bread, olive oil, and honey—the welcome spread of choice throughout our journey.).

Nora Rhandouss, Khadija Rhandouss, and Jihane share mint tea in Khadija’s salon in Khmisset.

“The techniques to make these mats are very old and very ancestral,” 60-year-old Fatiha Amalou, one of the artisans, tells me as we snack on a bowl of particularly glistening dates. We are sitting on a green and white patterned rug on the floor of another artisan’s house, where we’ve all gathered to chat. Not surprisingly, we’re also circled around a low table that, wouldn’t you know, magically appeared when we arrived. “The mats are so sacred that back in the old days, when people would die, we would wrap them up in them to take them away for burial,” Fatiha continues. “They were like a cape.”.

In a recent development, today, she is dedicated to preserving that sacred weaving tradition. But she also cares deeply about the craftsmanship itself. “Of course I want the legacy to continue; everyone wants the legacy to continue,” she tells me. “But really, perhaps more than anything else, I want to make something that makes me proud. We always say: If you make a good thing, it means you have a good head.” Another artisan, 51-year-old Khadija Rhandouss, nods in agreement. “When I make something good, I feel at peace,” she states. I tell them all that, as a bit of a perfectionist myself, I can relate to that sentiment wholeheartedly. Fatiha just laughs and smiles. “Yes, weaving is what we need to do to make money,” she says, “but it’s also part of what we do to feel good. It’s part of who we are.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that traditionally, cornbread stuffing requires making cornbread, cubing it and letting it dry out, mixing it with stock, eggs, meat, and aromatics, then transforming it into a stuffing (or dressing). This process produces some truly memorable casseroles, but I have an alternative that streamlines the process without compromising flavor: stuffing cornbread. It still smells enticingly like the classic Thanksgiving side as you set the baking dish on the table. I’ve still packed in a medley of woodsy herbs, sweet onions, vegetal peppers, and savory sausage. And it still slices into lofty servings to perch on your plate next to the sweet potatoes and green beans. It just takes half as long to make.

According to recent reports, the intentional two-to-one ratio of cornmeal to flour in this cornbread results in a moist, tender crumb that still has enough structure to hold up against the sturdy mix-ins. The sugar might seem like a lot, but it balances out the savory sausage and aromatics perfectly.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

According to recent reports, place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 400°. Line a 13x9" baking pan with parchment paper, leaving generous overhang on long sides. Coat pan and parchment with unsalted butter. Melt ½ cup (1 stick) unsalted butter in a large skillet over medium-low heat, then pour into a small bowl.

Cook 1 green bell pepper, halved, ribs and seeds removed, finely chopped, 1 medium white onion, finely chopped, and 2 celery stalks, finely chopped, in same skillet, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened, about 4 minutes. Add 1 lb. spicy and/or sweet Italian sausage, casings removed, and cook, breaking up and stirring occasionally, until browned (it may still be a little raw in the center at this point), about 5 minutes. Remove from heat.

Stir together 4 cups (624 g) fine-ground yellow cornmeal, 2 cups (250 g) all-purpose flour, 1 cup (200 g) sugar, 1 Tbsp. plus 1½ tsp. baking powder, 2 tsp. Diamond Crystal or 1¼ tsp. Morton kosher salt, 1 tsp. baking soda, and ¼ cup finely chopped sage, thyme, and/or rosemary in a large bowl. Gradually pour in 3½ cups buttermilk, then melted butter, stirring constantly until combined. Add 4 large eggs one at a time, mixing to incorporate after each addition. Fold in sausage mixture, then scrape batter into prepared pan.

Bake cornbread, rotating pan front to back halfway through, until golden brown and top springs back when gently pressed, 38–45 minutes. Let cool in pan 15 minutes. Using parchment paper overhang, lift cornbread out of pan and transfer to a cutting board. Cut into 12–18 slices; arrange on a platter.

Recent findings suggest that do Ahead: Cornbread can be baked 4 hours ahead. Store at room temperature; cut just before serving.

Industry observers note that mangos? No problem. Apples? Easy as 1-2-3. Any time I’m making a dish that needs something peeled in bulk, the Rotato is my go-to gadget. And my entire family has hopped on board.

Using it reminds me of putting on a record. You simply place your potato (or veggie of choice) on the spike at the bottom of the device, lower the top spike to hold it in place, and position the peeling blade against the top of the potato. Just press the red button, and the machine does the rest, automatically stopping when the cutter arm reaches the bottom.

And once you’ve watched it tackle a potato, it’s hard not to wonder what other fruits and vegetables you can try next.

According to recent reports, according to the Rotato’s instruction manual, it can also peel cucumbers, beets, turnips, avocados, eggplants, squash, zucchini, tomatoes, apples, pears, peaches, kiwis, lemons, limes, and oranges—way more than I even imagined. I’ll have to start dreaming up upcoming recipes.

#124108. Butter Mochi Cake With Maple-Miso Pecans

Butter Mochi Cake With Maple-Miso Pecans

📅 11 Jul 2023 | ⏱️ 3 min read (686 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Bonappetit

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family.
  • The batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake.
  • The secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for Shuai Wang, chef of King BBQ in North Charleston, South Carolina, mochi brings back memories of holidays with family. His other dessert love? Classic Southern pecan pie. This Hawaiian-style butter mochi cake draws on both, pairing a rich, chewy cake with a generous layer of maple-miso pecans.

The batter gets its signature bounce from mochiko, a distinct style of rice flour that gives butter mochi its chewy texture—not the fluffy crumb of a conventional cake. Coconut milk and melted butter add richness, while the pecans provide crunch. Let the cake cool completely before slicing so the texture has time to set.

The secret to the pecan topping is a little white or yellow miso, which brings savory depth to the maple syrup, much like the salt in salted caramel. The nuts need only a brief head start in the oven; they’ll continue to toast as the cake bakes.

Can I use regular rice flour instead of mochiko?

No. Mochiko, also called sweet or glutinous rice flour, has a different starch composition from regular rice flour. It’s responsible for butter mochi’s characteristic springy, slightly sticky chew. Regular rice flour or all-purpose flour won’t produce the same texture.

What kind of miso is best for baking?

Recent findings suggest that white and yellow miso are both good choices for this cake. White miso tends to be milder and slightly sweeter, while yellow miso has a somewhat more pronounced savory flavor. Either adds complexity to the maple-coated pecans without overwhelming their buttery, nutty flavor. Learn more about the different types of miso and how to use them.

Is butter mochi cake gluten-free?

Mochiko is naturally gluten-free, despite the sometimes confusing name glutinous rice flour. This recipe can be gluten-free, but check your miso: Some varieties contain barley or wheat. If you’re baking for someone who needs to avoid gluten, choose a miso labeled gluten-free and check your other packaged ingredients.

1 hour 30 minutes, plus cooling.

It has been revealed that place a rack in middle of oven; preheat to 350°. Lightly oil a rimmed baking sheet with vegetable oil. Whisk 2 Tbsp. pure maple syrup and 2 tsp. white or yellow miso (gluten-free if needed) in a medium bowl until smooth. Add 8 oz. raw pecans, coarsely chopped (about 2 cups) and 1 Tbsp. sugar and toss until evenly coated. Spread out on prepared baking sheet; bake until fragrant and matte looking, 6–8 minutes (nuts won’t be fully toasted). Let cool.

Lightly grease a 9"-diameter cake pan with unsalted butter and line bottom with a parchment paper round. Vigorously whisk 2 large eggs, 1¼ cups (250 g) sugar, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl until smooth. Add one 13.5-oz. can unsweetened coconut milk, well shaken, heated slightly if fat is solid, 2 tsp. vanilla bean paste or vanilla extract, and 6 Tbsp. unsalted butter, melted, slightly cooled, and whisk well. Add 1⅔ cups (254 g) mochiko and 1 tsp. baking powder; whisk vigorously until combined and batter is smooth and thick. Scrape batter into prepared pan.

Recent findings suggest that toss pecans to break up any clumps and scatter evenly over batter, going all the way to the edges (it may seem like a lot). Bake cake until sides start to pull away from pan, top is golden brown, and a tester inserted into the center comes out clean (some pecans will sink), 50–55 minutes. If pecans begin to brown too swiftly, loosely tent pan with foil. Transfer to a wire rack and let cake cool in pan 15 minutes. Turn cake out onto rack; peel away parchment and discard. Carefully turn cake right side up and let cool completely (at least 1 hour).

To serve, slice cake and top with scoops of vanilla ice cream.

Do Ahead: Cake can be made 1 day ahead. Store, loosely covered, at room temperature.

Ahead, you’ll have the chance to browse through some of the honorees’ best looks of 2026, with a snapshot of the key pieces that made those outfits stand out to us—and in turn, dominate the sartorial conversation at Vogue HQ. Some stars championed CFDA/Vogue Fashion Fund nominees early on: Edebiri and Lee both wore Lii for press appearances this year, while Lawrence sported one of Colleen Alleen’s velvet house coats with a white tee and slippers on a mild fall day in Upcoming York. Below, a snapshot of the wardrobes that make up Vogue’s Best Dressed list of 2026, complete with the key pieces needed to shop their signature looks and make them your own.

Industry observers note that A regular fixture in our weekly celeb outfits roundups, Jennifer Lawrence is known for her effortless brand of messy-chic, cool-mom-at-drop off looks, often centered around a ball cap and a slubby vintage tee. Pear Salad With Honey-Roasted Seeds

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake.
  • Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over.
  • For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the midst of a rich meal, something fresh and acidic keeps your taste buds awake. Where lettuce splashed with vinaigrette can feel like an afterthought, a juicy, savory-slanting pear salad is worth making room for on a plate full of turkey and cornbread. This is the antithesis of the haphazardly chunked together fruit salads you find at the supermarket for a brunch or dessert spread. Keep the focus on crisp-tart pears—apples also work—and it’s a welcome accompaniment to the other hearty dishes. Sliced razor-thin (use a mandoline) and fanned out on a platter, the fruit acts as an edible canvas for wisps of cheese and clusters of honey-roasted seeds. Leftovers (if you have any, of course) are delightful spooned over a well-toasted and buttered slice of multigrain bread the next day.

Pick firm green pears (Bartlett and Anjou are fair game; use Asian pears in a pinch) to ensure they hold their shape once sliced—even a little underripe is better than slightly over. After slicing, have a taste: If they are very tart, add 1 tsp. honey to the dressing; if fairly sweet, skip it.

For more Thanksgiving recipes, tips, menus, and inspiration, head to our 2026 Thanksgiving Hub.

Preheat oven to 325°. Whisk 3 Tbsp. honey, 1 tsp. garlic powder, ½ tsp. freshly ground pepper, 3 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil, and ¾ tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Add 1 cup raw sunflower seeds, pumpkin seeds (pepitas), and/or coarsely crushed raw nuts (such as walnuts, almonds, and/or hazelnuts) and stir to coat. Spread out in a single layer on a parchment-lined rimmed baking sheet; reserve bowl.

Recent findings suggest that bake seed mixture until golden brown, 12–14 minutes. (Honey mixture will puff up a bit but will deflate when you stir.) Toss honey-roasted seeds, then let cool. Toss again just to break up.

Industry observers note that whisk 3 Tbsp. fresh lemon juice, 1 tsp. Dijon mustard, a pinch of kosher salt, and remaining 1 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in reserved bowl. Add 2 lb. firm green pears (such as Bartlett and/or Anjou; about 4 large), cored, thinly sliced, to dressing and gently toss to coat.

Arrange pears on a large flat platter. Scatter honey-roasted seeds over and top with 2 oz. Parmesan, aged white cheddar, or Manchego cheese, shaved.

Do Ahead: Honey-roasted seeds can be made 6 hours ahead. Store at room temperature.

#124102. Which Thanksgiving Foods Belong in the Same Bite?

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Tasteofhome ↗ Open Full Page

Which Thanksgiving Foods Belong in the Same Bite?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (796 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Tasteofhome

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious.
  • For years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates.
  • Of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Taste of Home's Editorial Process.

Some Thanksgiving food combinations are obvious. Others might earn you some questioning looks at the dinner table.

For years, my kids refused to let any two foods touch on their plates. I found this particularly maddening at Thanksgiving. There’s an entire table of food to fit onto a single plate and only so much room to negotiate separate territories for the mashed potatoes and green bean casserole! Thankfully, they’re a little more accommodating these days and, like me, have come to appreciate the occasional overlap between dishes.

Of course, plenty of adults also have strong opinions about which Thanksgiving foods should mingle. There are those who insist on keeping every dish separate, those who permit a little gravy to stray onto the stuffing but draw the line at cranberry sauce, and those who deliberately assemble the perfect combination on every forkful. Then there’s always the unhinged relative who stirs the entire contents of their plate into a single, gravy-saturated mass and eats it with the serene confidence of someone who has never once questioned their choices.

In a recent development, personally, I’m firmly in favor of combining foods, although I do believe a little discretion is in order. Thanksgiving dinner offers a wonderful assortment of rich, savory and tart flavors, and knowing which ones to bring together is part of what makes the meal so satisfying. There’s a culinary reason that cranberry sauce belongs alongside turkey, and that stuffing and mashed potatoes are particularly good together. And once you understand why those combinations work, you can start building some excellent bites of your own.

Sources indicate that absolutely. In fact, some of the most familiar food pairings are built around the idea that one ingredient can supply something another lacks. Think of a rich cut of meat served with a sharp, acidic sauce, or a creamy dish finished with something crisp. Neither component is necessarily lacking on its own, but the contrast makes the combination much more interesting.

The same principle applies to Thanksgiving foods. Acidity helps balance richness, sweetness can temper salty or intensely savory flavors, and a change in texture can make a forkful more interesting. It’s not particularly complicated, but there’s a difference between understanding why two foods complement each other and simply hoping for the best.

Some combinations are simply better than others, though saying so at Thanksgiving dinner may invite more opinions than you bargained for.

Industry observers note that turkey and cranberry sauce: There’s a reason this pairing has endured for generations. Turkey, particularly the breast meat, is relatively mild, and the tartness of cranberry sauce gives it a welcome lift. It’s also an excellent remedy for turkey that’s spent a little too long in the oven, a situation that has befallen even the most conscientious Thanksgiving cooks.

Mashed potatoes, stuffing and gravy: I consider this one of Thanksgiving’s greatest achievements. The smooth, buttery potatoes and herbaceous stuffing are excellent together, and a generous spoonful of gravy makes the whole arrangement even better. There’s nothing particularly subtle about it, but Thanksgiving dinner isn’t generally celebrated for its subtlety.

In a recent development, sweet potatoes and turkey: The natural sweetness of roasted sweet potatoes makes a lovely contrast to savory turkey, particularly the richer dark meat. A traditional sweet potato casserole can work, too, although I draw the line somewhere around the marshmallow topping. I have nothing against marshmallows, but I prefer to encounter them after dinner.

It has been revealed that green bean casserole and mashed potatoes: These are two of my Thanksgiving essentials, and I see no reason they shouldn’t share a fork. The creamy green beans and buttery potatoes are lovely together, but it’s the crispy fried onions that really make the combination work. That salty crunch is a welcome addition to the softer textures.

According to recent reports, turkey, stuffing and cranberry sauce: This is probably my favorite combo of the bunch. The savory turkey and seasoned stuffing are practically made for one another, while a little cranberry sauce cuts through the richness. It’s essentially a Thanksgiving leftover sandwich without the bread, although I wouldn’t object to adding a dinner roll to the equation.

Industry observers note that macaroni and cheese and cranberry sauce: I realize this combination may call my culinary credentials into question, but hear me out. Rich, creamy mac and cheese practically begs for something sharp and acidic to cut through it, and cranberry sauce does exactly that. It’s not so different from serving a sharp cheddar with fruit preserves on a charcuterie board, although I concede that putting cranberry sauce on macaroni and cheese is a considerably harder sell. But that’s half the fun of Thanksgiving dinner: discovering which combinations you’re willing to defend.

Traditional bakeware usually features one primary material, such as aluminum, stainless steel or glass. Hybrid bakeware, on the other hand, takes a different approach by pairing multiple materials together. For example, durable stainless steel pairs with an easy-release ceramic nonstick coating. You get the best of both worlds in one pan.

In a recent development, stainless steel and ceramic nonstick make a pretty dynamic duo in baking. Stainless steel delivers durability and provides a sturdy baking surface, while nonstick helps prevent baked goods from sticking to the pan.

#124099. Ballerina Farm Is Opening a Restaurant, Farm Store, and Cooking School—Here’s a First Look

Ballerina Farm Is Opening a Restaurant, Farm Store, and Cooking School—Here’s a First Look

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 12 min read (2439 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~12 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, it’s a glorious late September morning in the Kamas Valley, and dozens of cows with handwritten name tags are circling me.
  • Industry observers note that still, the eloquence and enthusiasm with which he discusses the economics of small-scale agriculture surprise me.
  • According to recent reports, he speaks about each of the farm’s 120 animals with a fondness that belies his otherwise pragmatic approach to building a modern agricultural enterprise in America.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, it’s a glorious late September morning in the Kamas Valley, and dozens of cows with handwritten name tags are circling me. A soft breeze hints at the coming seasonal shift that will soon blanket this bucolic corner of Utah in frost. I’m standing beside two of Daniel Neeleman’s daughters and Daniel himself, a head full of curly hair and feet tucked into work boots. He exudes the easy familiarity of an old friend, despite a family name—and now a social media presence, thanks to Ballerina Farm’s 20 million-plus combined followers—that has taken on a life of its own.

Industry observers note that still, the eloquence and enthusiasm with which he discusses the economics of small-scale agriculture surprise me. “We love small agriculture and the diversification of it,” he says. “I think that we can make an impact in helping people see that small agriculture can work. Whether you’re doing an agritourism aspect or not, we still think it should and can be profitable.”.

According to recent reports, he speaks about each of the farm’s 120 animals with a fondness that belies his otherwise pragmatic approach to building a modern agricultural enterprise in America. Daniel did not grow up with animals, and still remembers how mesmerized he was the first time he saw a cow. “I tell people on the farm tours all the time, if your endorphins are going off watching these animals—watch out. You might be a farmer. It doesn’t go away, it might come back to you later in life.” From the very day that Daniel and his now-famous wife, Hannah, bought their first farm in 2017, he knew this was where they were meant to be.

Earlier that morning, I’m sitting at their kitchen dining table over a brunch of quiche, greens, yogurt, and just-picked mint tea, illuminated by beeswax spindle candles. “It’s our responsibility, and our love and passion too, to build this,” Hannah tells me, wearing a white dress with three daughters by her side. She’s sitting against a backdrop that’s become familiar to millions who have watched her cook and feed her growing family on a farm less than an hour outside of Salt Lake City.

Despite their sincere intentions, the Neelemans’ endeavor has brought moments of global controversy—the internet has scrutinized everything from how they homeschool their nine children to their family wealth to how they balance their roles as parents and cofounders. “We don’t take the platform that we’ve been given lightly,” Hannah says. Agriculture, she explains, has been at the heart of the project from the beginning, even as its reach has expanded far beyond the Kamas Valley. “It has worn a lot of different hats as it’s grown. We were young city kids, and we craved something real and knowing where our food comes from.”.

Now, what began as a story told online is becoming a universe people can actually step into themselves. On a stretch of land that spreads out beyond the window like something from “America the Beautiful,” they’re planning—and here announcing—one of the country’s most ambitious new farm hospitality destinations: a cookery school, farm-to-table restaurant, farm store, and spaces for agricultural education and events, all set within a working farm encompassing livestock, organic gardens, a dairy, and a forthcoming creamery.

At the heart of the vision is a cookery school, scheduled to open in 2029, that is as much about learning to cook from the farm as it is about taking those lessons home with you. The goal is to teach people how to cook seasonally and adapt when certain ingredients aren’t available, wherever they might live. (Daniel describes them as life skills rather than formal chef training.) “I want students to have time with the dairy, the market garden, the creamery, so they’re seeing where the food comes from,” Hannah notes.

According to recent reports, the cookery school will be guided by a similar philosophy to the legendary Ballymaloe Cookery School, where Hannah and Daniel spent 12 weeks in 2025—and first met Michael “Tiffin” Griffin, a beloved longtime instructor who has since joined Ballerina Farm as the director of the culinary experience. (A more formal, fine-dining restaurant may eventually join the school.).

Sources indicate that but visitors can step into the newly introduced Ballerina Farm world as soon as fall 2027, when a Dutch barn will open at the site of the current Kamas market. Inside will be a restaurant and cafe, referred to by the couple as an “eatery,” for meals featuring the meat, dairy, and produce grown on the surrounding farm—a considerable expansion of the current menus on offer at the Midway store and food truck.

Sources indicate that across a breezeway, a market will offer fresh produce straight from the garden and meat and dairy from the livestock—think onions, pea shoots, beets, ribeye steaks, smoked paprika goat cheese, and gallons of A2/A2 cream top whole milk—as well as a growing selection of prepared sides, sauces, and meals, from pickled torpedo onions to just-juiced turmeric ginger shots to chicken salad. The latter is Hannah’s particular favorite: “We got so attached to the chicken salad that we had this summer, because we grew meat chickens. We harvested them. And they made the most delicious chicken salad. Then Tiffin told us this week, ‘One more week of the chicken salad; I’m out of pickles. You’ll see it next spring.’ And I went, ‘Nooo,’” she laughs. “I think people are getting back to how grandma used to cook. She cooked from the garden, and it was amazing food.”.

In a recent development, just-cut spinach and radishes will sit next to Ballerina Farm's signature products that were initially only available online, as well as Ballerina Farm’s home goods like oven mitts, aprons, and wooden measuring spoons, all with the name appearing only discreetly. They also launched their first skincare product just this month: Tallow Tin body butter—made with tallow from the cattle, naturally.

It has been revealed that the restaurant, farm store, and a connecting courtyard will be more than five times the size of the existing Ballerina Farm store and cafe that opened in 2025, which sits 25 minutes down the road in Midway. “There’s an awful lot of hullabaloo about Hannah doing it, but for me, that’s what I saw when I was a kid. That’s how my grandmother lived her life,” Tiffin, the culinary director, tells me.

According to recent reports, over a two-hour meal of Ballerina Farm roasted chicken, garden carrots, pickled onions, and homemade yogurt, I sat enraptured by Tiffin’s story and the depth of knowledge and experience that had brought him to this particular farm in Utah. While guests can expect a diversity of dishes—Tiffin is especially passionate about Moroccan flavors—the land is the final decision-maker. “We’ll ask Tiffin what’s on the menu for an event,” explains Daniel, “and the first thing he'll say is, ‘Let me call Madison [Goodman], the head grower.’”.

Goodman is responsible for a vegetable operation that will eventually expand to five acres. The kitchen will draw on its harvest, but supplement it with neighboring producers when necessary—a philosophy similar to that which guided Tiffin at Ballymaloe: “If we can’t grow it, we get it locally. If we can’t get it locally, we’ll get the best.”.

The design and architecture of the project, meanwhile, will be led by Patrick Williams of Berdoulat, the British design house known for its richly textured, historically informed interiors. At Berdoulat, the mantra is “the house rules.” But as Williams puts it, “In this instance, where the buildings are yet to exist, the land rules.” His designs draw inspiration from 19th-century settlers’ homes and agricultural buildings in the Kamas Valley (and, yes, the family’s famous farmstead).

The Ballerina Farm team has worked closely with Kamas officials for years now to define what can be developed on its 14-acre property, prompting the city to introduce fresh agritourism zoning in 2024. The looks also protect the property’s conserved wetlands. “We are constantly in touch with the city,” indicates Brad Roberts, the brand’s director of marketing. If done well, Kamas can become a role model for the many other small towns grappling with their own decisions around the opportunities made possible through agritourism.

According to recent reports, yet the Kamas Valley is not the most obvious place to craft such an ambitious project that’s certain to draw travelers from not only the coasts but overseas. (Eighty percent of Ballerina Farm’s 10-million-plus Instagram following is based outside of the US.) A high water table can flood the gardens, frosts set in as early as October, and voles relentlessly try to work their way into the harvest. But the valley has a certain quality of light, giant skies, and an openness that feels rarer than ever in today’s world.

According to recent reports, walking through three high tunnels filled to the brim with produce, I eventually met Goodman, a fourth-generation farmer who ran his own successful CSA in the Kamas Valley, and was courted for years by the Neelemans before joining the Ballerina Farm team. He speaks passionately about the farm’s recently earned USDA organic certification, and the decades of advocacy that brought those standards into existence: “You can make me cry, because there are a lot of people who fought hard for this… the label helps us bridge this gap that we, as a society, have created between our reality,” Goodman notes, describing the certification’s baseline standards as the floor, while emphasizing that he’s reaching for the ceiling.

Recent findings suggest that “Everything here has a story,” he continues. “I can tell you the story of the winter leek. I can tell you the story of these girls.” (The girls are chickens.) He then spends 10 minutes explaining to me exactly why these chickens—Freedom Rangers rather than the more commonly raised Cornish Cross—are so special, and the process of raising them from chicks to harvest. “It’s hard for me to do this and not believe in a creator,” claims Goodman.

One of the challenges and opportunities of an agritourism project is that in a four-season destination like Utah, that experience will be remarkably different depending on when they arrive: tomatoes in the summer, spinach in the winter. Baby chicks in one season and a mature flock in another. “There’s something beautiful about eating what’s in season and retraining us as eaters to appreciate that,” reflects Hannah. “I have started to notice that I’m craving spinach, pumpkin, and squash because your body wants the things that are growing.”.

The culture side of agriculture has probably played a larger role in the Neelemans’ agricultural pursuits than they expected, however. While Hannah started sharing on social media as a way to kickstart business for their nascent pork operation, it snowballed into a public inquisition with what many perceived as an idealized, regressive performance of rural domesticity. But what the public wanted to know more than anything was how it was possible. What was real? And who funded it?

According to recent reports, when I ask them about balancing their ambitious vision with the realities of building a farm and business, Hannah says, “That’s a true founder of a manufacturer; they are the one who has to hold those two worlds together. We have to keep the dreams alive and the fire burning, but we’re also camping over the farm stand or dealing with broken pipes and trying to put up hoop houses.”.

Recent findings suggest that “We’re the ones that decide whenever there’s money left over at the end of the month from the business,” adds Daniel, who says that every individual part of the business is profitable. “We don’t have any investors, we don’t have any partners, it’s just us. So then it’s just a question of, ‘What projects are we going to conquer first?’ We are a for-profit company, and we have to be good stewards of the finances of all the things. It has to be sustainable,” he adds.

In a recent development, for years, people have been asking to visit, Hannah explains, sending her messages asking to meet the animals, help with chores, or simply spend a day on the farm. At the time, the Neelemans weren’t equipped to receive this audience of millions who had developed a relationship with a place they’d never visited. Now, they’re preparing to welcome both admirers and curious outsiders, as well as farmers and cooks, into the world that has generated so much conversation. “We have a community that wants to be a part of it,” Hannah recalls thinking. “So how do we build it?”.

Industry observers note that this fresh expression of Ballerina Farm places Hannah and Daniel among a lineage of visionaries in farm hospitality who have transformed working farms into gathering places—Ballymaloe, yes, but also Daylesford Organic in the English Cotswolds and Babylonstoren in South Africa. Though, of course, one important factor separates Ballerina Farm’s journey. Rather than building a hospitality destination and then finding an audience, the Neelemans are working the other way around. The relationship is already shaped by years of watching the family’s life unfold online—and by the very different ideas people have formed about what Ballerina Farm represents.

It’s easy to understand the appeal: Rather than watch a 60-second video on their phone, visitors can pull sourdough, or slip on a Ballerina Farm oven mitt and slide a pork chop out of the oven. They can greet a just-born calf. Their children can run the fields and breathe the fresh Utah air and taste the milk from Daniel’s cows. As I watched six Sebastopol geese waddle in front of the rental car while pulling through the gates of Ballerina Farm, even I felt that very modern feeling of disorienting familiarity upon experiencing a person or a place in the flesh that I had only ever seen on a screen.

Right now, the Kamas property has already begun hosting farm dinners, seasonal events, and agricultural experiences alongside the market and food truck. Each of these existing offerings showcases an element of how the Ballerina Farm world will eventually come together—market, meals, events, education, animals, and gardens all in one place.

According to recent reports, and for all the ambition of what Hannah and Daniel are building, the idea at its heart remains deeply personal. “The greatest work that we can do is in our homes and our own families and our communities,” Hannah tells me, a conviction that has remained constant even as Ballerina Farm's audience has rapidly grown.

Adds Daniel, “We’ve accomplished some things that we’re proud of, but we’re far from being done.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Unlike many iconic Italian recipes, this luxurious union of silky broccoli rabe, chile-flecked sausage, garlic, and curvaceous pasta is a weeknight hero. You can make it start to finish, in about 30 minutes. The key to successful execution is to go way beyond blanching when it comes to precooking the broccoli rabe in boiling salted water. For tender rabe that melds seamlessly with pasta and sausage, start by separating the thick stems from the rest of the stalks and giving them a head start before adding the rest. It removes any unpleasant bitterness and also means the rabe will cook into the saucy base of browned sausage and sweated garlic in just minutes.

While orecchiette is the traditional pasta choice, any short pasta will work. Sausage has become a popular addition to the true original Pugliese dish of stewed broccoli rabe with pasta, but a tin of anchovies makes a great substitute for added oomph and intensity.

This recipe is one of BA’s Best, our vault of the Test Kitchen's definitive takes on iconic dishes.

In a recent development, cut 2 large bunches broccoli rabe, trimmed, in half crosswise to separate thick stalks from thinner stems and florets. Cook thicker stalks in a medium pot of boiling salted water until crisp-tender, about 5 minutes. Add thinner stems and florets and cook until all of the broccoli rabe is tender (the tip of a paring knife should slide through the stalks with little to no resistance), about 3 minutes. Transfer to a rimmed baking sheet with tongs; let sit until cool enough to handle (no need to squeeze out excess water unless dripping wet). Coarsely chop into bite-size pieces.

According to recent reports, meanwhile, cook 1 lb. orecchiette (little ear-shaped pasta) or other short pasta in a second medium pot of boiling salted water until al dente (or use same pot with fresh salted water). Drain, reserving 2 cups pasta cooking liquid.

Industry observers note that heat 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil in a medium Dutch oven or other heavy pot over medium-high. Cook 1 lb. hot Italian sausage, casings removed if needed, breaking up with a wooden spoon, until golden brown and nearly cooked through, about 5 minutes. Add 1 head of garlic, cloves separated, peeled, thinly sliced, and remaining 2 Tbsp. extra-virgin olive oil. Cook, breaking up sausage even finer if needed and stirring often, until garlic is golden brown and softened, 3–4 minutes. Add broccoli rabe and cook, stirring occasionally, until very tender and wilted, about 5 minutes.

It has been revealed that add 4 Tbsp. (½ stick) unsalted butter, cut into pieces, pasta, and 1 cup pasta cooking liquid. Cook, stirring often and adding more pasta cooking liquid as needed, until pasta is coated in a clingy sauce. Taste and add some crushed red pepper flakes if desired. Add 1 oz. Parmesan, finely grated (about ½ cup), and stir, adding more pasta cooking liquid a splash at a time as needed to keep sauce smooth and shiny, until incorporated; season with salt.

Divide pasta among shallow bowls and top with more Parmesan.

Welcome to Open Tab, a weekly column covering the news, gossip, and stories that have stayed open in my tabs all week. Last time we covered the ever-escalating advent calendar wars.

It has been revealed that the long-awaited sixth installment of the Grand Theft Auto franchise was released this week. Why in God’s name am I talking about it for a food magazine? A Miami cafe even released a specialty roast of coffee beans, and one Florida restaurant chain partnered with Rockstar, the game’s developer, to bring an in-game food spot to life. (The game is set in a fictional state modeled after Florida.).

According to recent reports, this is the kind of widespread, obsessively orchestrated marketing strategy you’d expect around a Beyoncé album. We have arguably not been this close to a true monocultural moment since The Dress debate in February of 2015.

Industry observers note that in other news, Alison Roman’s podcast, Having People Over, which I teased in last week’s Open Tab officially debuted this week. Episode one features Bowen Yang, and the next couple will be with Lauren Graham and Jenny Slate—and then that’s it until 2027, as Roman told me.

Also in today’s Open Tab: the salty, salacious scandal around Maldon’s sourcing, a latest study on GLP-1s for children, the case for cocktail brutalism, and a Tuscon restaurant alchemizing desert ingredients.

At Bon Appétit, we love flaky Maldon salt. Like, we really love it. So when a report from The Observer detailed how Maldon’s famed UK sea salt was in fact also made with German rock salt, gasps rippled around the Bon Appétit office. I mean, not gasps exactly, but everyone was like “whaaaat? That’s crazy.”.

The gritty details: Maldon’s been harvested in Essex’s Blackwater estuary for more than a century, and the label on each box lists its only ingredient as 100% sea salt. The Observer’s report reveals that the organization imports mined rock salt from Germany as part of the “salt-on-salt” process in which the sea salt is enriched with minerals. The company is allowed to call their product 100% sea salt because the salt that comes from mines was at one point in a sea—in prehistoric times.

Origin and processing matters because these factors can affect the final flavor, color, and how salty it tastes. Maldon is a finishing salt, and it's largely prized for the crunch of its massive flakes. But consumers don’t love feeling like they’ve been lied to, and judging from the comments under Maldon’s apology post on Instagram, that is precisely how many feel.

I would wager that Maldon will survive this controversy. It’s a legacy brand that’s a staple in professional and home kitchens alike. And while it’s not a great look, I think the majority of consumers would say that salt is salt, and as long as Maldon stays crunchy and salty, they’ll be on board.

According to recent reports, semaglutide, the GLP-1 compound in brand name drugs Wegovy and Ozempic, is already approved for use in children older than 12. But a new study published in the New England Journal of Medicine highlights that the drug is effective for treating obesity in kids as young as six. According to the New York Times, drug manufacturer Novo Nordisk, plans to ask the FDA to authorize the drug’s use for kids in that age group.

In a recent development, it's hard to know what the long term effects on developed adult brains and bodies would be, let alone the quickly growing, changing brains and bodies of young kids. We’re beginning to see that GLP-1s can have a profound effect on mental health in adults, but though it seems the drugs can indeed contribute to weight loss in children, there are many other facets of its use that we simply don’t understand and haven’t studied yet.

According to recent reports, when I helped build our Best Bars list last year the question of what exactly makes a great bar was one we pondered over for many hours. Order a drink from a Bar of Note (i.e. one of the many bars sitting on a Best-of list somewhere on the internet), and you’ll quickly get a sense of how they answer that same question. Namely: spectacle.

Cocktails across the country and abroad have ramped up in complexity and presentation in recent years fueled mostly by the reason you might expect: spectacle and theatricality performs well on social media, according to a report in the Times.

According to recent reports, as a reporter who has often been forced to order the most attention-grabbing, loudest, most obnoxious drink on the menu in the name of journalism—and as a cocktail-enjoyer in my free time—I would like to propose a paradigm shift. Cocktail brutalism. Cocktail minimalism. Cocktail absurdism—actually anything besides the overwhelming maximalist cocktail moment that we’re stepping into. The ideal drink special? A beer, a shot, and a genuine compliment.

At Tuscon’s Ursa, ingredients from the surrounding desert are transformed. Chef Aaron Lopez and June Chee who lead the restaurant see cacti and brittlebrush as deeply flavorful staples of their menu. Read on to see how these ingredients come to life.

We’re on a mission to discover the hottest new groceries all year long, so when seasonal and limited-time items hit the shelves, you know we’re stocking up on the best of the best.

From stuffing-inspired potato chips to fizzy cranberry drinks, these are the holiday items worth seeking out the next time you’re at the grocery store.

“A hill I will die on? Cranberry is the best fall flavor. This soda has the fresh, fizzy bubbles I’ve come to expect from lemon-lime Poppi—but with a subtle twist. “Disclaimer: Peppermint is not normally my holiday flavor of choice. I’m much more into the eggnog and gingerbread of it all. It turns out that Sprouts found just the right balance of mint, bitter dark chocolate and just-sweet enough coconut milk—three flavors that I still can’t believe work this well together.

According to recent reports, texturally, these coconut rolls are outstanding. The light, crispy rolls, coated in snappy chocolate and crunchy snowflake sprinkles, are so easy to eat that I finished the entire bag in two days.” —Val Goodrich, food writer.

“I grabbed these stuffing-flavored kettle chips at the Trader Joe’s checkout line last week, and I need to go back to buy about 10 more bags. Bakeries are no longer just a stop along the way—they’re the final destination. According to Yelp’s 2027 Food and Drink Trend report, bakeries are becoming such a hot commodity that people are planning entire trips around viral treats. Yelp searches for “bakeries near me” are up 561% from last year, while searches for a “sweet treat” are up 303%. Treat yo’ self culture is officially here.

In a recent development, bakery tourism is on the rise, and honestly, I'm not surprised. I, myself, am prone to walking unfamiliar city streets just to get my hands on the town's most beloved pastry. And people are getting pretty specific about what they want. Searches for cardamom buns are up 24%, kouign-amann 67%, and salt bread a whopping 616%.

It’s not just individual pastries getting all the attention, either. Yelp found that searches for “hot and new bakeries” jumped 359%, while “best gluten-free bakery” rose 113%. Bakeries are also the most-saved type of specialty food shop on Yelp’s My Lists feature. Even New York City's Radio Bakery, which you’ll find below, saw searches increase by 176%. It seems we’re all doing some serious research before our next pastry run.

It has been revealed that so which hot spots should you add to your must-visit list? I asked Yelp to do a deep dive into the most-saved bakeries across America to see which ones people are bookmarking. Here's what came out on top.

This famed Taiwanese bakery opened its first U.S. outpost earlier this year in Pasadena, California, and has already gone viral for its unique cream cheese-filled bagels and flaky pastries.

It has been revealed that what started out as a pandemic-era creation has now morphed into a line-worthy brick-and-mortar. Bad Butter regularly draws block-long lines, with its breads, croissants, and pastries often selling out.

In Santa Ana, California, 61hundred Bread is known for its signature heirloom blue-corn masa sourdough bread, along with Filipino baked goods like pandesal and ube-filled cruffins.

In a recent development, at this Fresh York City French bakery, the jambon-beurre sandwich is the star item. Fresh baguettes and flaky croissants are also among the other reasons locals and tourists flock to the shop.

Located at the Halepuna Waikiki hotel in Honolulu, Hawaii, Halekulani Bakery is known for its signature coconut cake and assortment of pastries.

Located in Los Angeles, California, Out Of Ordi specializes in Korean-style salt bread.

New York City’s Sunday Morning frequently sells out of its viral cinnamon rolls.

San Diego’s Relic Bakery & Kitchen offers a mix of sweet and savory baked goods, from pies and croissants to breads and danishes.

In New York City, you’ll find Justin’s Salt Bread, voted the city’s best new bakery of the year and known for—you guessed it—its salt bread.

San Francisco’s Butter & Crumble is known for its crumble cakes and laminated pastries, with offerings that rotate seasonally.

In a recent development, another Honolulu bakery makes the list, although this one comes with a twist. Part bakery, part butcher shop, The Local General Store sells everything from quiche and danishes to sausage and ham.

It looks like my travel schedule just got a little busier (and tastier).

Veruschka, the Shape-Shifting Supermodel Who Defined an Era, Has Died at 87

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (998 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Vogue

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that richard Avedon famously pronounced Veruschka “the most beautiful woman in the world.” But what made the German model so mesmerizing was her seeming disinterest in preserving any one iteration of that beauty.
  • On November 25 it was confirmed by the German newspaper Bild that the model died at the age of 87, surrounded by friends and family at home.
  • It has been revealed that it was only earlier this month, on the occasion of the release of Ron Howard’s Netflix documentary Avedon, that Vogue revisited an extraordinary 25-page fashion editorial from its March 1, 1967, matter.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that richard Avedon famously pronounced Veruschka “the most beautiful woman in the world.” But what made the German model so mesmerizing was her seeming disinterest in preserving any one iteration of that beauty. She could be imperious or impish, feral or feline, androgynous or opulently feminine. She could contort her impossibly long limbs into unreal configurations, traversing fashion magazines and the wider public’s consciousness with ease in a way that had never been done before. One of the original supermodels, Veruschka was also among fashion’s great performance artists.

On November 25 it was confirmed by the German newspaper Bild that the model died at the age of 87, surrounded by friends and family at home.

It has been revealed that it was only earlier this month, on the occasion of the release of Ron Howard’s Netflix documentary Avedon, that Vogue revisited an extraordinary 25-page fashion editorial from its March 1, 1967, matter. Across those pages, Veruschka leapt and pirouetted, her hair fashioned into a long, swinging braid by hairstylist Ara Gallant. Avedon had found in Veruschka a woman who could give physical expression to his imagination and whose own imagination was every bit as expansive. Here was a woman whose beauty “demands something, and you must extend yourself to meet the challenge or know that a kind of splendor is lost to you forever,” said Avedon.

Born Vera Gottliebe Anna Gräfin von Lehndorff-Steinort on May 14, 1939, in Königsberg, East Prussia (now Kaliningrad, Russia), Veruschka’s early life was marked by the horrors of war. She was five years old when her father, Count Heinrich von Lehndorff-Steinort, was executed for his involvement in the failed 1944 plot to assassinate Adolf Hitler. The family was imprisoned by the Nazi regime, and the aristocratic world into which she had been born had all but disappeared by the time the war came to an end.

It has been revealed that an art student, she was discovered in Florence in 1959. Her early forays into modeling were not immediately fruitful: Standing over six feet tall, she was an unconventional proposition even then. An initial stint in New York proved disappointing, but in Italy she developed a fruitful creative relationship with photographer Johnny Moncada. Some 3,000 images from those formative years, undiscovered for decades, would eventually form the basis of the book From Vera to Veruschka: The Unseen Photographs by Johnny Moncada and an accompanying exhibition at London’s Somerset House in 2014.

Her greatest act of reinvention was, arguably, the creation of Veruschka herself. Adopting the Russian-sounding diminutive of her first name, she cultivated a persona of indeterminate provenance and mystique. Returning to Upcoming York in 1964, she found an industry increasingly receptive to her brand of beauty. In Diana Vreeland, then editor in chief of Vogue, she found a kindred spirit.

It has been revealed that the 1960s heralded the ascendance of a upcoming breed of model, with the likes of Jean Shrimpton, Twiggy, Donyale Luna, and Penelope Tree becoming cultural figures in their own right. Veruschka, with her high forehead, sculptural cheekbones, and elongated limbs, was one of the decade’s most arresting presences, whatever aesthetic she took on. She appeared on 13 American Vogue covers, working with the likes of Avedon, Irving Penn, Horst P. Horst, and David Bailey, and became one of the highest-paid models of her generation.

Sources indicate that some of her most enduring images were made in collaboration with the Italian photographer Franco Rubartelli, her creative and romantic partner. Among them was the indelible 1968 photograph of Veruschka in Yves Saint Laurent’s lace-up safari jacket for French Vogue, an image that distilled the designer’s newly introduced vocabulary of female sensuality and authority.

It has been revealed that veruschka was also an endlessly inventive beauty muse. The Vogue archives are rich with examples of her aesthetic adventurism. She sports fantastical lashes, intricately braided hair, graphic eye makeup, and elaborate headpieces. She was chameleonic, which made her popular with the hair and makeup artists of the era.

According to recent reports, and her fame extended well beyond the pages of fashion magazines. In Michelangelo Antonioni’s seminal 1966 film Blow-Up, set in Swinging London, Veruschka played a version of herself in a brief but electrifying scene opposite David Hemmings’s fashion photographer. A year later, she graced the cover of Life magazine. Few models before her had so thoroughly captured the imagination of the wider public, and her legacy lives on in the fresh generation of celebrity models today.

By the mid-1970s, however, Veruschka had grown disenchanted with the fashion industry. Her artistic ambitions began to take greater precedence over her modeling career. In collaboration with the German artist Holger Trülzsch, she embarked on a captivating body of photographic work in which her painted figure dissolved into architectural surfaces and natural environments, or assumed entirely different identities.

In 1971 Veruschka also appeared in West German magazine Stern with 27 other women under the coverline: “Wir haben abgetrieben!” (“We’ve had abortions!”) to advocate for abortion law reform at a time when it was illegal. It was a significant moment in Germany’s ’70s feminist wave.

Recent findings suggest that still, fashion never entirely relinquished its fascination with her, nor she with it. There were occasional returns to the runway, including for Chanel in 1994 and, at the age of 71, for Giles Deacon’s spring 2011 show in London. In 2017, Acne Studios enlisted her for its resort 2018 look book. In contemporary photos—with her silver hair slicked back, sporting oversized, louche tailoring—she looks every bit as modern as she had half a century earlier.

Veruschka on the red carpet at the Berlin Film Festival in 2015.

Much has been made of Veruschka’s otherworldliness, but there was something profoundly human in her commitment to metamorphosis. At the height of her fame, she could have made a career out of being the most beautiful woman in the world. How much more interesting, instead, to become a thousand different women.

Industry News: Dirty Spaghetti
