📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that dark matter is hypothetical matter that makes up the large majority of the matter in the Universe, but we can't see it because it doesn't interact with light.
  • According to recent reports, primordial black holes are hypothesized to have formed in the first fractions of a second after the Significant Bang, from the direct collapse of pockets of dense matter.
  • The research is "The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes," and it's published in The Astrophysical Journal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that dark matter is hypothetical matter that makes up the large majority of the matter in the Universe, but we can't see it because it doesn't interact with light. Scientists put their minds into hyperdrive trying to understand it and figure out what it is. One of the proposals is that primordial black holes (PBH) account for some or all of dark matter.

According to recent reports, primordial black holes are hypothesized to have formed in the first fractions of a second after the Significant Bang, from the direct collapse of pockets of dense matter. Really small PBHs wouldn't have survived this long because of Hawking Radiation, but more massive ones could have. New research focuses on asteroid-mass PBHs and how they could be detected, if they exist.

The research is "The Life and Death of Stars that Capture Primordial Black Holes," and it's published in The Astrophysical Journal. The lead author is Ore Gottlieb, an assistant professor of physics at MIT. The authors focus on what are called Hawking stars, stars that have engulfed a microscopic PBH. They're named after renowned physicist Stephen Hawking, who first proposed them in the 1970s.

Sources indicate that "Primordial black holes (PBHs) in the asteroid mass window (1017â1023 g) remain viable dark matter candidates and can be captured by stars," the authors write. Though it's all theoretical at this point, the researchers developed a framework for what would happen to stars that capture these PBH. They used stellar evolution models, simulations, and other tools to try to understand what would happen.

Primordial Black Holes are only theoretical, so far. But if they exist, they could find their way inside main sequence stars. Image Credit: NASA and G. Bacon/STSCI.

First of all, a single star on its own is unlikely to capture a PBH. But a star with a stellar or planetary companion would have enough gravitational interactions to trap a PBH in one of the stars. It could take thousands or even millions of year for a PBH to work its way into a star's center.

According to recent reports, âThen, this is where the action begins,â remarked lead author Gottlieb. Once the PBH reaches the center, the star can't survive.

Sources indicate that according to this work, there are two outcomes for stars that suffer this misfortune, and both spell doom. "We find that the fate of these systems bifurcates: PBHs that form an accretion disk before consuming the host drive explosive disruption, whereas PBHs captured too late or growing too slowly consume the star quietly," the authors write.

Sources indicate that once a PBH finds its way into the center of a star, it takes only a few million years before it consumes about 1% of the star's mass. Then, the rotation rate comes into play. If it's fast enough, the star's gas can't fall directly into the PBH. Instead, an accretion disk forms around the PBH, inside the star. This is where the two outcomes diverge.

âInside the star, you have a black hole with a disk,â Gottlieb said. This is an almost unimaginable scenario, but the research reveals it's possible.

âThe black hole is also spinning, and itâs twisting space and time.â.

The PBH then warps the star's magnetic fields, and just like in a SMBH, powerful jets are introduced. âThis twisted magnetic field will power very strong electromagnetic jets from the poles of the black hole,â Gottlieb explains.

What star could survive powerful jets being emitted from inside?

According to recent reports, âOnce the disk forms, this is essentially a death sentence for the star,â mentioned lead author Gottlieb. The authors write that this produces "an explosive Hawking-star transient powered by a rapidly spinning PBH." The PBH emits jets that tear through the star, promptly destroying it.

âAnd these jets will just explode the star, within a few dozen seconds," Gottlieb mentioned. "Itâs very fast. Once you have a disk, you are done.â.

This schematic illustration shows the evolutionary sequence of a Hawking star. First the PBH is captured, and eventually it migrates into the stellar core. Once the PBH is embedded in the core, the PBH grows by accreting stellar mass. What happens next depends on whether the PBH forms a disk before it consumes its host. If a disk forms, that warps the magnetic fields, and the PBH debuts jets from inside the star, destroying it in seconds. If no disk forms, the star dies a quiet, gradual death, and a stellar-mass black hole is left behind. Image Credit: Ore Gottlieb et al 2026 ApJ 1012 157.

In the second case, the star's destruction is less cinematic. "The system dies quietly," the authors write, "leaving a PBH with mass of the order of the consumed stellar mass and little or no bright disk-powered emission." It's basically a stellar-mass black hole indistinguishable from others of its kind.

These two paths to destruction create different prospects for observing PBHs engulfed by stars.

According to recent reports, "Our results carry important observational implications across both electromagnetic and GW channels," the authors explain. "If a PBH has grown sufficiently to form an accretion disk, the associated disk winds and relativistic jets can inject enough energy and momentum into the stellar envelope to unbind the star and power an explosive transient.".

The rapid destruction creates a bright transient that emits EM radation across multiple wavelengths. This could be detectable at long distances with modern telescopes, similar to supernovae.

Sources indicate that âWe would initially detect some X-rays and gamma rays, then over time optical and infrared emissions, and later on radio emissions,â Gottlieb claims. âThis is something we could potentially detect, if itâs not happening too far from us. It could be many galaxies away, not just in our backyard.â.

This simulation depicts the moments after a primordial black hole is captured by a star. As soon as the black hole falls into the starâs center, it creates a swirling disk of material (orange). Within a matter of seconds, interactions between the black hole and the spinning disk should launch powerful jets of matter that ultimately pierce through the star, making it explode.

GWs from these events are likely more rare. Scientists have long wondered if PBH could be GW sources, and it's possible that the Hawking-star remnant that's left behind could be detected as one if it ever formed a compact binary with another compact object. The authors say that if this happens, it's exceedingly rare. But if it does happen, observing them would be very informative. "Thus, GW detections would be highly diagnostic if found, but should be regarded as a binary-evolution-limited and likely subdominant discovery channel for Hawking stars.

Here's where dark matter comes in. These Hawking-stars, if they exist and can be detected individually, could be used to calculate their population. If these stars work the way the researchers think they work, they can be detected and used to "provide independent observational constraints on the PBH population," the authors write. But on the other hand, "the absence of such transients or of convincing subsolar merger candidates could constrain the fraction of DM in PBHs.".

So it seems there's a potential viable pathway to detect dark matter, if indeed PBHs are real and astronomers can find them destroying a star in a telltale blinding flash.

In a recent development, âThere is hope for us to probe primordial black holes through interactions with stars,â Gottlieb remarked. âWe expect this to be visible, and itâs something we should look into.â.

A 72-Year-Old Invention Could Be the Key to Unlocking More Powerful Quantum Computers

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1000 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A technology older than the laser is finding fresh life inside diamond, offering a potential way to make quantum computers more powerful without overwhelming their sensitive measurement systems.
  • In a recent development, A quantum computer can process information using the strange rules of quantum physics, but getting an accurate answer out of it presents a challenge.
  • Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have developed a new amplifier that tackles this problem using an unlikely material: diamond.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A technology older than the laser is finding fresh life inside diamond, offering a potential way to make quantum computers more powerful without overwhelming their sensitive measurement systems.

In a recent development, A quantum computer can process information using the strange rules of quantum physics, but getting an accurate answer out of it presents a challenge. The information is carried by extremely faint microwave signals that must be amplified before they can be measured. Unfortunately, amplifying those signals can introduce unwanted noise, making it harder to tell what the computer is actually saying.

Researchers at the Okinawa Institute of Science and Technology (OIST) have developed a new amplifier that tackles this problem using an unlikely material: diamond. Their device can strengthen microwave signals more than 1,000 times while adding very little noise. It can also handle stronger signals and operate in magnetic fields, potentially overcoming limitations that make today’s quantum computers difficult to scale up.

The findings were published on November 16, 2026, in Nature Communications.

Sources indicate that in superconducting quantum computers, information is stored in quantum bits, or qubits. To determine a qubit’s state, researchers measure a weak microwave signal associated with it. The difficulty is that these signals are extraordinarily sensitive to interference.

That is one reason superconducting quantum computers operate at temperatures close to absolute zero, the lowest temperature theoretically possible. Keeping the equipment this cold reduces interference caused by heat, but it cannot eliminate the noise introduced by the amplifiers themselves. Once that unwanted noise enters the measurement, subsequent amplification stages strengthen it along with the original signal, increasing the chance of an incorrect reading.

Sources indicate that existing amplifiers can detect these faint signals with remarkably little added noise, although they come with trade-offs. Conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers, for example, can become overwhelmed when several qubits are measured simultaneously. This effect, known as saturation, limits how many signals they can reliably process at once.

According to recent reports, another technology, known as kinetic inductance parametric amplification, can handle stronger signals but generally requires more electrical power and additional wiring. As quantum computers grow, that extra equipment adds cost and complexity. Some systems also use qubits based on electron spin, which require magnetic fields that can disrupt conventional superconducting amplifiers.

The OIST researchers approached these challenges by revisiting a technology that predates the laser.

Masers were first demonstrated in 1954, six years before lasers appeared. Both technologies amplify electromagnetic waves, but while lasers work with light, masers operate with microwaves. They rely on a process called stimulated emission, in which an incoming photon carrying the right amount of energy prompts an excited electron to release another matching photon. Repeating this process strengthens the original signal.

“Despite being invented before optical lasers, masers — microwave lasers — have been left far behind because they often require cryogenic conditions to function, which made them impractical until very recently,” explains Dr. Yuimaru Kubo, head of the Hybrid Quantum Device Team at OIST. “But now, with quantum computers operating at temperatures very close to absolute zero, we have given them upcoming life as very promising candidates for amplifying quantum signals with very little noise.”.

Industry observers note that to put this older technology to work, the team used a specially prepared diamond containing nitrogen impurities known as P1 centers. These impurities contain electrons whose spin, an intrinsic quantum property, makes them behave like tiny magnets.

The researchers apply a relatively weak microwave field to the diamond, supplying energy that pushes most of these electron spins into higher-energy states. When a faint microwave signal enters the amplifier, it stimulates the excited spins to release their stored energy as additional microwaves at the same frequency.

In effect, the diamond transfers energy from its excited electrons into the incoming signal, making that signal stronger without requiring a powerful microwave source.

“We were surprised by how much amplification we could achieve using such a small amount of microwave power,” adds Kubo.

According to recent reports, in testing, the diamond maser amplified microwave signals more than 1,000-fold while introducing just 2.55 quanta of added noise. Quanta are discrete units used to describe energy at the quantum scale. For comparison, the fundamental quantum limit for this type of amplification is 0.5 quantum, meaning that even an ideal amplifier cannot eliminate added noise entirely.

Industry observers note that the device also tolerated much stronger incoming signals than conventional Josephson parametric amplifiers. Because the diamond maser operates in a magnetic field, it could be particularly useful for quantum computers that rely on spin-based qubits.

It has been revealed that although the technology is still being developed toward commercialization, its potential uses extend beyond quantum computing. Sensitive microwave amplification is also key in spectroscopy, which scientists use to investigate the properties of materials, and nuclear magnetic resonance, the physical principle behind MRI scanners.

Other possible applications include fundamental physics experiments searching for dark matter, where detecting extremely weak signals could help researchers investigate one of the universe’s most elusive mysteries.

In a recent development, reference: “A near-quantum-limited diamond maser amplifier operating at millikelvin temperatures” by Morihiro Ohta, Ching-Ping Lee, Vincent P. M. Sietses, I. Kostylev, J. R. Ball, P. Moroshkin, T. Hamamoto, Y. Kobayashi, S. Onoda, T. Ohshima, J. Isoya, Hiroki Takahashi and Yuimaru Kubo, 16 November 2026, Nature Communications. DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-79021-7.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that senate Majority Leader John Thune arrives for a GOP conference meeting at the Capitol on Tuesday. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call).

Senate Republicans on Tuesday were weighing whether to postpone their leadership elections after what several senators described as a “frank” conversation about their midterm losses last week.

But so far, no official candidate has emerged to challenge John Thune, R-S.D., for the post of minority leader in the newly introduced Congress.

The conference was supposed to begin its leadership elections Tuesday morning, but pushed those back to hear from members still reeling from the midterm results, which saw the GOP lose their Senate majority. As the conference meeting turned into what some dubbed an “open-mic session,” they took a break to attend previously scheduled committee hearings, with a initiative to return at 2 p.m. Next they must decide whether to forge ahead and pick leaders Tuesday or to punt those choices to a different day.

In a recent development, sen. Josh Hawley, R-Mo., stated the conversation taking place was “honest” and “frank.”.

According to recent reports, “I will vote for the delay,” he remarked. “We’ve got a lot of things that we’ve got to think through, and I think to rush into this and to just ratify all the same leadership — I mean, what message does that send?”.

It has been revealed that “If you don’t think after losing seven seats minimum that we need to change course, I don’t know what planet you’re on,” he stated, adding he was frustrated that his party didn’t do more to focus on topics like affordability ahead of the midterms. “I know it’s easy to blame other people, but we need to look at what has happened here.”.

Sources indicate that sen. Ron Johnson, R-Wis., who is leading the charge to delay the leadership elections and collected signatures to call the conference meeting beforehand, called it “a very high-quality conversation” in which he was “leading.”.

“People are voicing opinions on all sides of the challenges. It’s one of those times in the Republican conference where you kind of go, ‘We’ve got some smart people, and we’re having a very good, respectful conversation.’”.

No challenger to Thune, the current majority leader, stepped forward during the closed-door meeting, several senators remarked. Sen. Kevin Cramer, R-N.D., said “they’re not even criticizing Thune” inside the room. “It hasn’t been about John Thune.”.

“It’s been about the family,” Cramer mentioned, describing it as a “family discussion.” Thune and others in leadership had yet to speak, as the candidate forum hadn’t started yet.

Sen. Rand Paul, R-Ky., remarked voters reacted to high gas prices, the war in Iran and the cost of living.

According to recent reports, “The cost of living defeated us,” Paul remarked. “I don’t think anybody in Texas who voted for the Democrat governor was voting against John Thune. If you diagnose that as a problem, you’re misdiagnosing the problem.”.

Hawley didn’t say how long he’d like to see a delay. “Long enough for people to think through this, and if there’s somebody else … or several somebodies who want to run for positions, let them think through it.”.

Cramer was asked if senators in the room were placing any blame on President Donald Trump over how he handled midterm messaging.

“There was a lot of discussion about the president,” Cramer said.

Tech Report: Latest Research Reveals Europa's Sodium Cloud Originated from its Interior Ocean

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1128 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, jupiter's moon Europa has been fascinating astronomers and astrobiologists for decades.
  • Keck Observatory in Hawai'i have revealed something newly introduced and very surprising.
  • It has been revealed that their results, reported in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics, provide the first connection between the two, giving scientists a more complete view of the moon's environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, jupiter's moon Europa has been fascinating astronomers and astrobiologists for decades. Ever since the Voyager probes passed through the system in 1979, scientists have theorized that an ocean lies beneath its icy crust. Further observations bolstered this theory, revealing surface plumes caused by warm water pushed up through vents in the crust (cryovolcanism). They've also found fascinating chemistry on the moon's surface, and an enormous, diffuse cloud of sodium surrounding it.

And now, observations by the W.K. Keck Observatory in Hawai'i have revealed something newly introduced and very surprising. That sodium cloud has remained remarkably stable after more than two decades of observations despite the dynamic and powerful forces that characterize Jupiter's environment. In a recent study led by Boston University, an interdisciplinary team of researchers compared sodium measurements high above Europa with observations of sodium clouds very close to the surface.

It has been revealed that their results, reported in the Journal of Geophysical Research: Space Physics, provide the first connection between the two, giving scientists a more complete view of the moon's environment. This, in turn, gives scientists a sneak peek at the ocean beneath Europa's surface. The team's observations relied on two decades of observations using Keck's High Resolution Echelle Spectrometer (HIRES) instrument, allowing them to map the sodium cloud's distribution and how it responds to changing conditions in the system.

In a recent development, europa's sodium cloud is oblong-shaped, elongated in the east-west direction, and measures over 46,800 km (29,095 mi) in diameter, or about 30 times Europa's radius. Sodium is of particular interest to planetary scientists because it is a constituent of sodium chloride (salt), a key ingredient in Earth's oceans. Based on the latest fossil evidence, scientists theorize that life first emerged approximately 4 billion years ago in Earth's primordial oceans around hydrothermal vents.

It has been revealed that based on multiple lines of evidence, astrogeologists also believe that similar vents exist inside Europa at the core-mantle boundary. Understanding the origin and distribution of sodium around Europa can help researchers learn more about the materials on the moon's surface and potentially subsurface. Emma Lovett, a graduate student at Boston University and lead author on the study, explained in a W.M. Keck Observatory release:.

We don't know a lot about Europa's hidden ocean and icy surface, but its atmosphere offers a window into this potentially habitable world. The whereabouts of life beyond Earth might be closer than we ever imagined.

Recent findings suggest that however, studying sodium close to the moon's surface presents many challenges. Foremost among these is the highly reflective nature of Europa's surface ice, which can overwhelm the faint signal emitted by nearby gas. To overcome this problem, the team used the HIRES instrument's high-resolution, long-slit configuration to measure the sodium's distinctive spectral fingerprint. They also observed Europa as it passed through Jupiter's shadow, ensuring that there was no direct sunlight reflecting off the surface to interfere with the signals they detected.

By changing the instrument's orientation at multiple locations, the team mapped the sodium cloud rather than measuring its spectra at any single point. Lastly, they combined new observations with archival data Keck obtained in 1999 to see how the cloud changes over time. Surprisingly, they found that the cloud has remained stable despite changes in Jupiter's plasma environment and the influence of the neighboring volcanic moon Io, which spews sodium into space. Remarked Carl Schmidt, a researcher at Queen's University Belfast and Boston University:.

The neighboring volcanic moon Io sprays sodium around the Jupiter system, and we've often wondered if Io paints Europa's surface. The stable sodium abundance in these Keck data indicates that Europa is indifferent to Io's volcanic activity. What we observe originates in Europa's saltwater and not in Io's volcanoes.

In a recent development, radiation from Jupiter can break apart molecules on Europa's surface. This can free oxygen, which could percolate in brines through the surface into the ocean under the ice. Credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech.

A particularly beneficial observation occured on September 29th, 2022, when NASA's Juno spacecraft passed behind the moon relative to the team's perspective. For the past ten years, Juno has studied Jupiter's atmosphere, magnetosphere, and plasma environment. So on this occasion, the team had the chance to study the sodium cloud alongside measurements of the local plasma cloud. This enabled the team to examine the sodium cloud across a range of conditions and to test the effects of Jupiter's magnetosphere and Io's volcanic activity.

While most astrobiology missions are presently searching for evidence for past life on Mars, Europa is the next target in the search for extraterrestrial life. Right now, NASA's Europa Clipper mission and the ESA's JUpiter ICy Moons Explorer (JUICE) are en route to the system to study this icy moon. Because Europa is not a terrestrial planet but an "Ocean World," it offers major opportunities to study potentially habitable environments beyond Earth. In particular, scientists want to see how water and other materials are transferred between the surface and the interior.

Sources indicate that while no direct evidence of organic molecules has been detected on the surface, research strongly indicates the moon has the key chemical ingredients and pathways to form them. And while the sodium cloud does not provide a direct measurement of Europa's ocean, understanding its origin and behavior helps scientists understand the moon's chemical environment. Building on their momentum, the team is at the moment using the Hubble Space Telescope to look for magnesium in Europa's atmosphere, another possible element in Europa's ocean salts. As Lovett summarized:.

These observations help us refine our models of Europa's atmosphere, testing what releases sodium and how radiation pressure shapes its distribution. We're also looking for magnesium, which has been tentatively detected on Europa's surface but not yet in its atmosphere. Finding it could provide another notable clue to the salts present on this intriguing ocean world.

Breaking: This Common Vitamin Deficiency Could Be Quietly Disrupting Your Sleep

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (653 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A study combining blood tests and wearable sleep monitors suggests that a common vitamin deficiency may play an overlooked role in sleep health as we age.
  • It has been revealed that older adults with higher vitamin D levels slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night and experienced shorter periods of nighttime wakefulness than those with lower levels, according to a study led by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health.
  • The findings suggest that vitamin D may be an crucial factor in sleep health as people age.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A study combining blood tests and wearable sleep monitors suggests that a common vitamin deficiency may play an overlooked role in sleep health as we age.

It has been revealed that older adults with higher vitamin D levels slept nearly 20 minutes longer each night and experienced shorter periods of nighttime wakefulness than those with lower levels, according to a study led by researchers at the Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health. Vitamin D deficiency was associated with an even greater reduction in sleep duration.

The findings suggest that vitamin D may be an crucial factor in sleep health as people age. However, the researchers caution that the study cannot establish whether increasing vitamin D levels directly improves sleep.

“These findings suggest that we should investigate more thoroughly whether boosting vitamin D levels can improve sleep health,” indicates study senior author Adam Spira, PhD, MA, professor in the Department of Mental Health at the Bloomberg School and a core faculty member of the Johns Hopkins Center on Aging and Health.

The researchers, working in collaboration with scientists at the National Institute on Aging, analyzed data from 460 men and women with an average age of approximately 71. Participants were assessed between 2012 and 2019 as part of the Baltimore Longitudinal Study of Aging. Blood samples provided measurements of vitamin D concentrations, while wrist-worn actigraphs recorded sleep and wake patterns.

After accounting for age, race, sex, and other potentially influential factors, the researchers found significant associations between higher vitamin D concentrations, longer sleep duration, and less prolonged nighttime awakenings.

When participants were classified according to clinical definitions of vitamin D deficiency, insufficiency, and normal levels, those with a deficiency slept approximately 23 minutes less than those with normal levels.

Sources indicate that both vitamin D deficiency and disrupted sleep are widespread among older adults. Poor sleep has been associated with an increased risk of dementia, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and other chronic conditions. Earlier studies have also linked low vitamin D levels to poorer sleep quality, although clinical trials investigating the benefits of supplementation have generally involved small and relatively homogeneous populations.

In the latest study, the associations between vitamin D concentrations and sleep appeared strongest among Black participants.

“Black adults in the United States have a higher prevalence of vitamin D deficiency and sleep disturbances compared to white adults, and may benefit more from increasing vitamin D levels,” says study first author Diefei Chen, a PhD candidate in the Bloomberg School’s Department of Epidemiology.

The team also investigated vitamin B12, which previous research has suggested may influence sleep. Women with higher B12 concentrations tended to spend less time awake after initially falling asleep. Among men, higher concentrations appeared to be associated with more nighttime wakefulness. Neither pattern was supported by conclusive statistical evidence.

The researchers could not determine whether participants obtained their vitamin D primarily through sunlight exposure, food, or supplements. Future investigations could examine whether these different sources influence sleep differently.

The study used a serial cross-sectional design, meaning that researchers analyzed a series of snapshots over time rather than establishing how changes in vitamin D levels affect subsequent sleep patterns.

Further research, particularly larger clinical trials and studies tracking changes in vitamin D and sleep over extended periods, will be needed to determine whether correcting a deficiency can meaningfully improve sleep in older adults.

Reference: “Association of vitamin D and B12 levels with actigraphic sleep in cognitively unimpaired middle-aged and older adults” by Diefei Chen, Jill A Rabinowitz, Fan Wu, Zhikui Wei, Yang An, Jennifer A Schrack, Toshiko Tanaka, Chee W Chia, Mark N Wu, Sarah K Wanigatunga, Luigi Ferrucci, Eleanor M Simonsick and Adam P Spira, 14 October 2026, The Journals of Gerontology: Series A. DOI: 10.1093/gerona/glag212.

Support for the research was provided by the National Institute on Aging (T32AG000247, R01AG050507, HHSN-260-2004-00012C).

You don’t really need a holiday occasion to bake a pie, but it doesn’t hurt to let the spirit of the season introduce you to a few more festive recipes. Whether you’re a fan of savory dishes, prefer fruit pies, or love the wobble of a perfectly set custard pie, there is a pie for everyone — including Eater staffers.

Sources indicate that we love a super-easy no-bake pie just as much as we love a more complex, picture-perfect creation. Here are some of our favorite pie recipes to make at home this holiday season and beyond.

Since I grew up in Los Angeles and had never heard of buttermilk pie, it may come as a surprise that it’s one of my go-to pies to make. I discovered it seven years ago on a Twitter thread about unique, regional pies and was fascinated enough by this classic Southern dessert to attempt it, trying the first recipe that came up on my Google search. This is that recipe, and it has been consistently easy and perfect since that very first pie I made. The filling is smooth and velvety with subtle notes of nutmeg and a kiss of lemon. It reminds me of dan tat, or Chinese egg tarts, but it’s way less fussy. Yes, you can make your own pie crust, but storebought works well here, too, because the real star is the wobbly buttermilk custard. — Kat Thompson, audience editor.

When fall comes around, I turn to this tried and true caramelized onion and butternut squash tart from Food 52 over and over again. It’s a perfect savory option to bring to Friendsgiving, Thanksgiving, or any autumnal get together. What I love most about it is that it highlights flavors and ingredients of the season while standing out from the plentiful pumpkin and pecan pies that you’re sure to find at any gathering. To make it heartier, I sometimes add crumbled sausage to the mix. — Terri Ciccone, deputy director of audience development.

In a recent development, the only thing my mom and I love more than re-invigorating this incredibly simple chess pie recipe is telling the (most likely made up) story behind the name. Trying on my grandmother’s Texas twang, we explain how a server at a diner was once asked the flavor of the custard pie that day. She said, “It’s just pie,” but with her Southern accent that was mistaken as “chess pie.” And so we got this simple custard pie, which is filled with evaporated milk and set perfectly with cornmeal. My mom started experimenting with adding edible lavender oil to the recipe, which has became my favorite way to bake it, but she’s also added a tablespoon or two of my dad’s “Mexican mocha” (spiced hot chocolate) mix to make an incredible chocolate custard pie with a kick. But even plain, this pie recipe is always a significant hit. — Emily Venezky, social media manager.

Industry observers note that I have nothing but the utmost respect for people who lovingly make intricately crafted, high-maintenance pies with lattice crusts and the whole shebang, but my personal tried-and-true, always-go-back pie recipe is one I’ve frequently revisited since high school: no-bake chocolate peanut butter pie. I do not know the true origin of the semi-homemade, Sandra Lee-esque creation, but if you stumble upon some version of the five-ish-ingredient recipe that includes Cool Whip, like this one on the blog Crazy for Crust, that’s what I’m referring to. Rest assured that I generally have the taste and standards of a bougie person, but this extremely simple, absolutely-not-healthy recipe is just perfection. It’s sweet, salty, creamy, and simultaneously light, fluffy, rich, and decadent. Whenever I make it for a dinner party, holiday gathering, or potluck, it garners rave reviews (the word “orgasmic” has been used to describe it more than once). And as a child of the ‘90s, I love using an Oreo crust and Skippy peanut butter — forever crowd-pleasers. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.

“We have Milk Bar at home, honey” is what comes to mind whenever I make this pie, which reminds me of the Upcoming York City bakery’s famous, albeit once salaciously named dessert (now called the Milk Bar Pie). This butterscotch pie from Smitten Kitchen packs the same gooey, buttery taste and a satisfyingly sticky consistency — I feel like it’s a pie for people who wish they could just eat caramelized graham cracker crusts and custards for dessert. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

Anna Theoktisto, Southern Living.

According to recent reports, this zingy citrus pie might evoke summertime, but that’s exactly why I make sure it’s on the table during the holidays. Somewhere between a lemon pie and an icebox pudding, Atlantic Beach Pie delivers the bracing acidity I crave after a marathon of rich food. It originated at a North Carolina seafood restaurant, acting as a clever loophole to the old wives’ tale that eating dessert after a seafood meal could be deadly. Believe the lore or not, this pie is bound to earn seconds, whether for its salty, buttery saltine crust, zippy custard filling, or cloud of velvety whipped cream. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Claudia Fleming, adapted by Amanda Hesser for the Latest York Times.

I am not a pie person, per se — I hate the pressure of making a flaky crust — but I don’t mind the less-stress approach of making a tart, which asks only that I press dough into a tart pan. This famous chocolate caramel tart, a version of which my mom made frequently when I was growing up, is a dish I would definitely have on my roster if Mythical Kitchen ever invited me onto Last Meals. With dark chocolate ganache, a caramel filling that’s made more complex by the addition of salt and creme fraiche, and a sprinkling of a little more flaky salt on top, it tastes like a slightly more sophisticated Twix Bar.

Recent findings suggest that I once asked my mom to make it for an ex-boyfriend, with me talking it up to him as my favorite dessert ever, and when he told me it was “just okay” — and who claims that, especially when presented with a free dessert that required the dessert-giver to make a caramel? — that was the final sign I needed that he was not the one for me. Lesson learned: My husband and I are very dessert-compatible. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Josh Walker & Duolan Li, Bon Appétit.

#123974. Making Sense of Chaotic Supernova Ejecta With the JWST

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 8m • 📚 Deep Dive (1681 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Universetoday ↗ Open Full Page

Making Sense of Chaotic Supernova Ejecta With the JWST

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1681 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that finding order in the chaotic aftermath of a supernova explosion isn't easy.
  • In a recent development, massive stars play an notable role in the evolution of the cosmos.
  • Astrophysicists can't see inside stars to learn more about this process, so they have to wait until they turn themselves inside out and then examine the results.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that finding order in the chaotic aftermath of a supernova explosion isn't easy. But the JWST has the tools to do it. Its Mid-Infrared Instrument (MIRI) and its Medium-resolution Spectrometer (MRS) were built for situations like this.

In a recent development, massive stars play an notable role in the evolution of the cosmos. They're responsible for synthesizing astronomical metals, the elements heavier than hydrogen and helium that are necessary to form everything from rocky planets to living organisms. Without massive stars, the cosmos would look much different. It would be a simple mixture of hydrogen, with a little helium mixed in, and trace amounts of lithium. Nature can't build planets or create life with that limited palette.

Astrophysicists can't see inside stars to learn more about this process, so they have to wait until they turn themselves inside out and then examine the results.

Recent findings suggest that massive stars live fast and die young, then explode as supernovae. When that happens, the explosion sends their contents, including their astronomical metals, out into the interstellar medium. Once there, it's available not only for planets and life, but for the next generation of stars.

Recent findings suggest that when a supernova explodes, it leaves behind a supernova remnant, the matter ejected by the explosion in an expanding shockwave. The shockwave heats up the expanding shell, creating some of Nature's most stunning displays. The shocks can also rebound, creating an inward shock wave. It can create a real mess, but there are still patterns to be discerned. Within the exanding shell, molecules come form that tell astrophysicists what happened inside the star prior to its explosion.

Industry observers note that one of the most well-known supernova remnants is Cassiopeia A (Cas A). It's about 11,000 light years away, and it was observed by Earthlings around 1667. Astronomers are interested in it because they can learn a lot about the exploding star that created itâthe progenitorâby analyzing its contents.

The JWST was built for just such an endeavour. In latest research in The Astrophysical Journal Letters, a team of researchers used the JWST's MIRI and MRS to determine Cas A's chemical makeup. The research is "JWST Resolves Dust Emission from Individual Ejecta Clumps in Cassiopeia A: Dominant Grain Compositions Point to a Shell Merger in the Progenitor," and the lead author is Tea Temim, a research scientist from Columbia University.

According to recent reports, "We present a study of dust emission in the supernova remnant (SNR) Cassiopeia A (Cas A) observed with the MIRI Medium-resolution Spectrometer (MRS) on board JWST," the authors write. "The unprecedented spatial resolution at mid-IR wavelengths allows us to isolate dust emission from individual arcsecond-scale clumps of supernova (SN) ejecta and circumstellar material (CSM) and identify the dominant dust species in each chemically distinct region.".

Sources indicate that massive stars fuse different elements in layers, and that's reflected in the remnants they leave behind when they explode. Increasingly heavier elements are forged in the core, up until iron is reached. Lighter elements are fused together in the surrounding layers. These layers tell the star's history, but it all gets blown into space when the star explodes as a supernovae. To make matters more complicated, these shock waves can bounce back as reverse shocks.

Sources indicate that the clumps in the supernova ejecta that the authors refer to are huge, as large as our Solar System. In studying these clumps with the MRS, the researchers were able to identify different dust species region by region, rather than as one mixed up jumble of spectra. They learned that the progenitor star underwent a shell merger.

Recent findings suggest that âMaterial within these shells churns and circulates, which can cause the shells to merge shortly before the supernova explosion,â lead author Temim remarked in a press release. âSo, for example, this would be something like the oxygen- and carbon-burning shells in a star merging together and changing the structure of the star significantly. And that would then change the chemical abundances that you would see after a supernova explosion in the ejecta of a supernova remnant.â.

Before they turned to the JWST, they used Spitzer images to identify regions to focus on with the JWST.

This figure highlights Spitzer images on the left and JWST images on the right. The JWST obviously has a much higher resolution, and the researchers used it to map Cas A's dust chemistry all across the remnant. The observations led to a better understanding of the shell mergers the remnant went through right before it exploded, and a better understanding of the progenitor's overall structure. Since astrophysicists can't see inside stars, they have to wait until they turn themselves inside out. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, JPL-Caltech, T. Temim (Columbia University), R. Arendt (UMBC), D. Milisavljevic (Purdue University). Image Processing: A. Pagan (STScI).

Industry observers note that the Spitzer identified regions with different dust properties. The researchers focused on three of them with MRS.

In a recent development, "The MRS spectra extracted at positions P1, P2, and P3 ... all exhibit significant emission from warm dust, but with spectral shapes that differ considerably between the three regions," the authors write.

It has been revealed that this image shows the overall supernova remnant and the locations of three regions with distinctly different dust properties first identified with the Spitzer Space Telescope. The researchers examined these regions more closely with the JWST's MRS, seen as P1, P2 and P3. Image Credit: NASA, ESA, CSA, Danny Milisavljevic (Purdue University), Tea Temim (Princeton University), Ilse De Looze (UGhent); Image Processing: Joseph DePasquale (STScI).

Sources indicate that P1 samples reverse-shocked ejecta that has bright argon emissions dominate by grains of SiO2 (silica). It helps the researchers track the outer layers of the supernova's ejecta. Finding it supports the idea that the progenitor underwent a carbonâoxygen shell merger.

Recent findings suggest that P2 is centered on what astronomers call Cas A's "Green Monster" structure, which is the green structure near the center. It's emissions are attributed to circumstellar matter emissions on Cas A's near side, not material from Cas A's progenitor. It's likely made of mostly Mg2SiO4, which helps astronomers determine that the progenitor's dust and the CSM dust are distinct from one another.

In a recent development, P3 is another reverse-shocked region. It has very bright neon emissions compared to P1. That favours another shell merger, this time between a carbon shell and an oxygen shell.

This image of Cas A is from the JWST's MIRI F2100W filter. The P1, P2, and P3 regions are indicated by the white arrows. "The spatial distribution of the P2-like emission associated with Mg2SiO4 CSM dust is shown in green, P1-like emission associated with SiO2 dust is shown in magenta, and P3-like Ne-rich emission associated with carbon dust is shown in blue," the authors write. Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26.

"Identifying the different types of dust grains formed in the chemically distinct layers of a supernova brings us one step closer to understanding how much dust supernovae contribute to the interstellar dust reservoir in our galaxy," mentioned co-author Ilse De Looze, associate professor at Ghent University in Belgium. "By revealing the composition of this newly formed supernova dust, JWST also provides crucial insights into how well these grains can survive the powerful reverse shocks that sweep through the supernova debris, ultimately determining how much dust can escape into the interstellar medium.".

Industry observers note that this JWST image of Cas A has the synchrotron emissions subtracted. Since synchrotron emissions are non-thermal, and since their emission lines overlap the lines from thermal dust, removing them helps to isolate the signal from the ejecta, which is what the researchers are interested in. So this image basically tracks the thermal emissions from carbon dust. Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26.

The JWST played a leading role in this effort to piece together what happened to Cas A's progenitor. But it's observations added to an existing observational base from JAXA's XRISM x-ray satellite and NASA's own Chandra X-ray Observatory. Taken together, the more complete picture shows that the progenitor's shell mergers were underway prior to its explosion as a supernova.

Industry observers note that after all the imaging, processing, and fitting to models, this is the overall result. This figure shows which parts of the Cas A ejecta are from the existing circumstellar medium (left: Mg2SiO4 grains) and which parts are actually form the progenitor star (right: SiO2 grains.) Image Credit: Tea Temim et al 2026 ApJL 1012 L26.

âWith Webb, the vast improvement in being able to resolve at the individual clump level helps us do more sophisticated dust chemistry,â remarked Dan Milisavljevic, associate professor and co-author of the study from Purdue University in the United States. âAs a result, we can tie the explosion back to the makeup of the progenitor star hundreds of years afterward. Itâs telling us about what was happening, we think, in the hours leading up to core collapse. Understanding this process is essential to explaining which elements the supernova explosion will release into the galaxy and how those elements enrich future generations of stars and planets.â.

These results will also help build better model for understanding other supernova remnants.

The authors say this work shows how important the JWST's high-resolution images are for understanding dust ejecta in supernova remnants and how it was formed. (But smart Universe Today readers already know how important the JWST is.).

"It also demonstrates that spatially resolved dust compositions in young SNRs can serve as a powerful probe of the chemical structure and explosion properties of core-collapse SNe," they conclude.

A Surprising Newly introduced Treatment Prevented Type 1 Diabetes in 55% of Mice

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, an experimental treatment using tiny particles released by stem cells has delayed the onset of type 1 diabetes in mice, offering a potential way to protect insulin-producing cells from immune attacks.
  • Developed by UCLA researchers, the approach targets the immune response responsible for type 1 diabetes rather than simply controlling blood sugar.
  • The research drew inspiration from pregnancy, when a mother’s immune system typically tolerates a developing embryo despite its genetic differences.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, an experimental treatment using tiny particles released by stem cells has delayed the onset of type 1 diabetes in mice, offering a potential way to protect insulin-producing cells from immune attacks. In a 90-day study, 55% of mice receiving the particles through a slow-release gel remained diabetes-free.

Developed by UCLA researchers, the approach targets the immune response responsible for type 1 diabetes rather than simply controlling blood sugar. The findings, published in Nature Nanotechnology, suggest that naturally occurring particles called extracellular vesicles could help preserve pancreatic function. The treatment remains experimental and has not been tested in humans.

The research drew inspiration from pregnancy, when a mother’s immune system typically tolerates a developing embryo despite its genetic differences. Scientists wondered whether stem cells might produce substances capable of preventing harmful immune responses.

In a recent development, “Nature has designed something amazing,” remarked senior author Song Li, a professor of bioengineering at UCLA and member of the UCLA Broad Stem Cell Research Center. “If we can better understand how an embryo avoids rejection by the mother’s immune system, it could be very useful for a lot of immune-related diseases.”.

Sources indicate that li’s team investigated extracellular vesicles, microscopic particles that transport proteins, lipids, and genetic material between cells. They compared vesicles from embryonic stem cells and induced pluripotent stem cells, or iPSCs, with those from mesenchymal stem cells, which are known for their immune-regulating properties.

Experiments involving human and mouse immune cells demonstrated that vesicles from pluripotent stem cells had stronger anti-inflammatory effects than those from mesenchymal stem cells.

The particles also promoted the development of regulatory T cells, specialized immune cells that help prevent attacks against healthy tissue. Further analysis identified distinctive proteins, lipids, and genetic material that may contribute to these effects.

To test whether the vesicles could protect against diabetes, the researchers transferred immune cells capable of attacking insulin-producing pancreatic cells into mice, then treated the animals with iPSC-derived vesicles.

In a recent development, because extracellular vesicles rapidly disappear from injection sites, the researchers developed an injectable hydrogel that gradually releases them over several days. The treatment was administered beneath the skin near the neck, allowing the particles to interact with immune cells in nearby lymph nodes.

Those immune cells could then circulate throughout the body, potentially reducing attacks on pancreatic tissue.

Recent findings suggest that two treatments with the vesicles, either alone or in the hydrogel, significantly delayed diabetes onset compared with untreated mice. After 90 days, 55% of mice receiving the hydrogel formulation remained diabetes-free. They also had more regulatory T cells in their lymph nodes and retained more insulin-producing pancreatic tissue.

In a recent development, “One thing that surprised us was that a local injection could provide protection throughout the body,” Li noted. “That’s the beauty of this approach.”.

Producing enough extracellular vesicles for future therapies presents a major challenge. To address this, researchers grew stem cells in three-dimensional clusters suspended in gently moving liquid instead of on flat laboratory surfaces.

The method increased vesicle production 3.4-fold per million cells while preserving notable particle characteristics. Because iPSCs can multiply extensively in the laboratory, they could provide a more reliable source of therapeutic vesicles than adult stem cells.

Industry observers note that the treatment may be most effective during the early stages of type 1 diabetes, when some insulin-producing cells remain functional. Suppressing the immune attack could help preserve these cells and maintain natural insulin production.

“In the early stages, you still have some pancreatic cells left,” Li noted. “If you can regulate the immune cells, you may be able to keep the remaining cells functional.”.

Industry observers note that for patients who have already lost most of these cells, immune regulation alone would not restore insulin production. However, the approach might help protect transplanted insulin-producing cells from rejection.

Recent findings suggest that researchers blueprint to evaluate the treatment in larger animal models, investigate dosing and long-term effectiveness, and determine whether it could weaken defenses against infection. The findings may also inform future treatments for other autoimmune diseases and strategies to protect transplanted cells.

The leaders of an effort to overhaul how the House deals with sexual misconduct hope their proposal will see action before the end of the 119th Congress, though they’re split on the odds.

Rep. Kat Cammack, R-Fla., chair of the Republican Women’s Caucus, noted legislative text is done and is being looked at by the relevant committees.

“Yes, absolutely,” she said when asked if the package would get a vote this year. “We’re shopping it now with the different committees, House Admin and Ethics, and waiting on their final feedback, which we should have actually this week.”.

Recent findings suggest that rep. Teresa Leger Fernández, chair of the Democratic Women’s Caucus, stated she was still optimistic about getting it done, but stopped short of putting full faith in Republican leadership to get it over the finish line. The effort has been underway since May, when Cammack and Leger Fernández’s caucuses revealed a partnership to propose changes after two members of the House resigned amid allegations of sexual misconduct.

Asked if she thought Speaker Mike Johnson would put the proposal on the floor during the busy lame-duck session, Leger Fernández laughed.

“Hopefully, that’s something that will happen, because you know the Republican Women’s Caucus had mentioned they were optimistic before we left. I’m still optimistic,” she said.

Industry observers note that the two groups have spent months holding dozens of meetings with staff, their own caucuses and male members of Congress, among others. Suggestions have included banning members of Congress from engaging in sexual relationships with any House staffer, not just those who work for them directly, and outlining penalties for violaters. Initially, the groups were expected to unveil their work by August recess, but that got pushed back as the House canceled weeks in session and as they cited a desire to get it right.

Cammack said she thinks Johnson “has been very sincere in his efforts on this.”.

According to recent reports, “That would be a tremendous disappointment” if he didn’t put it on the floor, she remarked when asked about the possibility. “I genuinely believe he cares about this issue.”.

Leger Fernández said if it doesn’t get done by the end of the 119th Congress, she hopes some changes would be adopted under the rules package for the next Congress that Democrats bring forward in January. Such packages are typically adopted with party-line votes and give incoming majorities the chance to tweak how the House operates to their liking. While certain narrower proposals aimed at curbing sexual harassment could be written into House rules, others would need to pass both chambers and be enacted into law to take effect.

“We are going to move to make sure it is in the rules package, because we will be in charge next year,” Leger Fernández remarked. “But I would love for it to pass now, because that was a commitment that it be bipartisan.”.

One Tiny Protein Change Could Help Explain Severe Childhood Epilepsy

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (701 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Scitechdaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism that helps position a protein linked to severe childhood epilepsy within nerve cells.
  • According to recent reports, A single change in a protein associated with severe childhood epilepsy can dramatically alter where it resides inside nerve cells, according to new research from the University of Liverpool.
  • Recent findings suggest that the study focuses on CDKL5, a protein essential for normal brain development and function.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Scientists have uncovered a previously unknown molecular mechanism that helps position a protein linked to severe childhood epilepsy within nerve cells.

According to recent reports, A single change in a protein associated with severe childhood epilepsy can dramatically alter where it resides inside nerve cells, according to new research from the University of Liverpool. The discovery suggests that some neurological disorders may arise not only from impaired protein activity but also from proteins failing to reach the locations where they are needed.

Recent findings suggest that the study focuses on CDKL5, a protein essential for normal brain development and function. Mutations in the gene that produces this protein cause CDKL5 deficiency disorder (CDD), a rare genetic condition characterized by severe seizures beginning in infancy and significant developmental difficulties. The disorder affects approximately 1 in 40,000 to 60,000 live births worldwide.

Despite years of research into CDKL5, scientists have struggled to understand how the protein is organized within nerve cells and why certain mutations have such devastating neurological consequences.

A research team led by Ben Goult, Professor of Mechanistic Cell Biology at the University of Liverpool, identified a previously unknown molecular docking mechanism that anchors CDKL5 to the structural framework of synapses, the specialized junctions through which nerve cells communicate.

Disrupting this anchoring mechanism altered the organization of nerve cells. The researchers also discovered that even a remarkably small modification to the protein could interfere with its positioning.

Dr. Yasumi Otani, first author of the study and former PhD student in the Institute of Systems, Molecular and Integrative Biology, said: “What was particularly striking was that changing just a single amino acid at the very end of CDKL5 was enough to dramatically alter its localization in nerve cells. This indicates just how critical the final residues of the protein are for keeping CDKL5 in the right place at synapses.”.

Sources indicate that the researchers also uncovered an unexpected connection between CDKL5 and the mechanical forces generated within cells. CDKL5 binds directly to talin, a protein capable of changing its shape in response to physical forces.

In experiments using cultured cells, interfering with this molecular interaction or reducing the forces produced by the cells changed the distribution of CDKL5. The findings suggest that cellular mechanics may help regulate where CDKL5 carries out its biological functions.

Recent findings suggest that many genetic mutations associated with CDD produce shortened versions of the CDKL5 protein that lack the newly identified docking sequence. These mutations may therefore disrupt neurological function partly by preventing CDKL5 from reaching its intended location, rather than solely by impairing its enzymatic activity.

Professor Ben Goult stated: “Much of the research into CDKL5 deficiency disorder has focused on the activity of the enzyme itself. Our work highlights another potentially crucial factor: where that activity takes place. By identifying the molecular interactions that position CDKL5, we can begin to understand how the protein is organized within synapses and why disrupting this organization might interfere with communication between nerve cells.”.

According to recent reports, the research, conducted in collaboration with scientists at the University of Helsinki in Finland, establishes a molecular framework for investigating how defective protein positioning contributes to CDD. It also opens a potential avenue for therapeutic research, although whether restoring CDKL5 localization could improve neurological function remains unknown.

In a recent development, andreas Borg, founder of CURE5, a parent-led foundation dedicated to finding a cure for CDKL5 deficiency disorder, mentioned: “Seeing how profoundly CDKL5 loss affects so many systems in the body also gives us hope that new opportunities for therapeutic intervention remain to be discovered. The new understanding of the protein’s location and function identified in this work opens up one such possibility. As parents, even the smallest improvements in our children’s lives mean the world.”.

A Star’s ‘Obliquity’ Likely Has Little Impact On A Given Planet’s Habitability

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1133 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Universetoday

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumplanetary disk which surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity.
  • The angle between the spin axis of a star and the orbital axis of its planetsââstellar obliquityââholds clues about how the spin-orbit orientations of stars and planets evolve throughout their lifetime, Lauren Biddle, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told me via email.
  • In a paper accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal, Biddle and her co-author, Brendan Bowler, compared stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single sunlike stars.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A star's axial tilt as it relates to the circumplanetary disk which surrounds it is known as stellar obliquity. Over space and time, there are a myriad of solar type stars with all sorts of obliquities. But the question heretofore has always been what effect a given starâs initial obliquity has on the planetary system that forms around it.

The angle between the spin axis of a star and the orbital axis of its planetsââstellar obliquityââholds clues about how the spin-orbit orientations of stars and planets evolve throughout their lifetime, Lauren Biddle, an astrophysicist at Princeton University, told me via email.

In a paper accepted for publication in The Astronomical Journal, Biddle and her co-author, Brendan Bowler, compared stellar inclinations with orbital inclinations for 114 single sunlike stars.

Biddle and Bowler sampled 49 protoplanetary disk systems where planets were just beginning to form around their nascent stars. They also sampled 24 debris disk systems (stars circled by rings of gas, dust, and rocky planetesimals).

Sources indicate that the authors then sampled 21 warm Jupiter systems (where gas giant planets circle their parent stars on orbital periods that range between 10 and 100 days). And finally, they sampled 20 so-called hot Jupiter systems. Hot Jupiters were the first type exoplanets found around sunlike stars and usually orbit their parent stars on insanely short orbits of less than ten days, but at least one has been found to orbit its parent star in only 16 hours.

Yet as Biddle notes, the processes that drive changes in stellar obliquity could differ depending on a combination of how close a planet is from the central star and how old the planetary system actually is.

This work tests for signatures of obliquity evolution across âspaceâ by comparing the spin-orbit angles of planetary systems across a range of orbital distances, and âtimeâ by comparing systems over a range of ages, Biddle told me.

The results show that stellar obliquities are similar across orbital separation and age.

This suggests that after planets form, it is rare for their orbits to undergo large changes, and the changes that do happen are not detectable in the current data, notes Biddle.

Some theories predict that orbital inclinations of planets could drastically change over time due to gravitational interactions with other planets or stars; or in the case of hot Jupiters, interactions from tidal forces with the host star, states Biddle. We donât see that in our data; instead, we find that the fraction of misaligned orbits in young planetary systems resembles that of older ones, she says.

It has been revealed that by âstellar misalignment,â Biddle means that the starâs spin axis points in a different direction than the orbital axis of a planet. In contrast, a system is aligned when the starâs equator lies in the same plane as the planetâs orbit, like a spinning top placed at the center of a hula hoop.

Sources indicate that it is misaligned when the starâs spin axis is tipped relative to that plane, says Biddle. But because of observational limitations, we can only measure the lower limit of the angle between a starâs tilt and the orbitâs tilt, she says.

So, the true difference could actually be larger.

It has been revealed that thus far, however, large stellar obliquity changes appear to be uncommon. But Biddle notes that there is a major caveat in their data.

We deliberately chose single stars that are cooler and host giant transiting planets, claims Biddle. We left out stars with close stellar companions, hot stars, small planets, and non-transiting giant planets on wider orbits, so large tilts could be common in any of those, she says.

This artist's conception demonstrates a binary-star, or two-star, system, called HD 113766, where astronomers suspect a rocky Earth-like planet is forming around one of the stars. At approximately 10 to 16 million years old, astronomers suspect this star is at just the right age for forming rocky planets. The system is located approximately 424 light-years away from Earth. Credit: NASA/R. Hurt, JPL-Caltech/C. Lisse, JHUAPL.

In practice, every system we classified as misaligned is tilted by at least 10 degrees, and on average the misaligned ones are tilted roughly 30 to 50 degrees, notes Biddle.

A Plethora Of Strangely Mis-Aligned Exoplanets.

But prior to the discovery of extrasolar planets, our understanding of these alignments was based entirely on the organization of the Solar System, where planets are mostly aligned with the Sun, with the large ones orbiting farther out, says Biddle. So, it came as a surprise when we discovered that giant close-in exoplanets with very misaligned orbits exist, she says.

Our own solar systemâs planetary alignments are pretty much coplanar.

The Sunâs spin axis, however, is tilted by about 6 degrees relative to the average orbital plane of the planets and dwarf planets, states Biddle.

Biddle doesnât know for certain if the Sunâs axis was tilted from the start.

Industry observers note that but if we assume it started out aligned, there are several proposed explanations for how the Sun could have become tilted, notes Biddle. They include a past fly-by of another star, tugs from an undiscovered distant planet, torques from stellar winds, and even internal gravity waves, she says.

Recent findings suggest that there isn't evidence that stellar obliquity itself affects planetary habitability, indicates Biddle. But it does tell us about the history of planets' formation and where they eventually end up around the host star, which matters a lot when it comes to habitability, she says.

Every year, my sister and I have a stuffing-off. Not that we’re all that competitive (we are), but she insists on having her signature mushroom and sage stuffing, and I insist on making the best stuffing. My recipe is just an old Gourmet magazine version of sausage cornbread stuffing with a bunch of fennel, but what makes it exceptional is my own riff on what is so often overlooked as filler when it comes to stuffing (or, depending on where you’re from, dressing): the bread cubes. I take the full loaves of Whole Foods’ signature cornbread, slice them into cubes, stick them in a low oven (around 200 degrees) for a few hours, and eureka! It’s a stuffing that delivers again and again.

Why are the store-bought loaves the key? I’m not quite sure. My hunch is that they’re just dense enough, un-fresh enough, and mass-produced enough to dry out easily, and the store’s recipe strikes some unicorn balance of flavor that compliments the fennel without making the dish overwhelmingly sweet. — Lesley Suter, brand director.

Industry observers note that I keep coming back to this deeply savory, unexpected side dish when the weather turns cold. Its varying textures, ample acidity, and subtle sweetness are a welcome addition to any spread of holiday sides. Cabbage and bacon might be a familiar pairing, but the miso paste and Dijon that are swirled into the reduction offer a pleasant and welcome surprise to the palate. An added bonus: Jesse’s videos are some of the most relaxing and soul-soothing I’ve seen on the internet; it’s as if he invented food ASMR himself. Let them regulate your blood pressure this holiday season when that one in-law’s antics start to send you over the edge. — Nat Belkov, deputy brand director.

Nobody says they crave a salad at Thanksgiving, but I promise you they do, especially once the heaviness of everything else starts to set in. At the very least, I crave a salad at Thanksgiving, and the kind of salad I desire in an instance like this is something crunchy and bright and which tastes nothing like anything else on the table. Thus, some combination of citrus and fennel is generally my go-to. The citrus lends a brightness that pairs well with the cranberry sauce that’s inevitably on my plate, and I like the licorice sweetness of fennel amid the savoriness that dominates the spread; plus, I think it goes well with the celery that’s in other dishes.

While more complex takes on this kind of salad exist and sound delicious, I find the most pared-down versions easier to slot into my day of cooking. This salad is usually my very last task before we sit down to eat. Sometimes, I don’t even announce that it’s happening, so it seems like the “just threw this together,” afterthought touch that surprises you with how essential it ends up being. — Bettina Makalintal, senior reporter.

Tauba Auerbach, Salad for President by Julia Sherman.

Recent findings suggest that tauba Auerbach’s Brussels sprouts salad recipe in Julia Sherman’s book Salad for President is a pleasing salad with lots of crunchy textures and punchy flavors that’s become a go-to of mine for the holidays. Thinly shaved Brussels sprouts serve as the base of the salad, while lemon-marinated, toasted almonds add bite to the equation. The dressing adds tartness with sherry and cider vinegars, which is a nice juxtaposition against the season-sweet apple pieces. Don’t skip the pickled mustard seeds if you have the time, as they add another dimension of flavor. — Dianne de Guzman, regional editor, Northern California/Pacific Northwest.

Recent findings suggest that this is less of an elaborate recipe, and more of a plea: Please don’t bring steamed green beans to Thanksgiving dinner (or any holiday, for that matter). They’re hardly offensive, but I’ve always found them to taste a bit ghostly and one-note. Instead, I like this simple but impactful recipe of garlicky green beans. High-heat oil, garlic, and ice cubes at-the-ready will give you crispy green beans with a welcome, garlicky char to liven up the usual parade of sweet potatoes and all the beige classics. — Francky Knapp, staff writer.

I have become the Sweet Potato Bringer at our family’s large, outdoor potluck Thanksgiving, mostly because I am the only one who must have them (or it’s not Thanksgiving, obviously). Every year, I bring a sweet potato casserole with essentially the same elements: mashed sweet potatoes — slow-roasting them in the oven lends a deeper flavor — brightened with things like orange juice or cinnamon applesauce; some sort of pecan-y crumbly brown sugar topping; and blistered marshmallows. It’s all very satisfying but can become somewhat formulaic, which is why, a couple years ago, I kicked it up a notch with Epicurious’s s’moresy take on the classic: In this recipe, the sweet potato mixture gets added earthiness from maple syrup and unsweetened cocoa powder, while the pecan topping’s punch-up is the addition of crushed graham crackers (you can buy them gluten-free to be more inclusive). It’s not a dramatically different flavor from the original, meaning the eternal crowd-pleaser lives on. — Nicole Fellah, dining editorial manager.

Mitchell Davis, Cook and Eat Better.

If I am having a holiday party with a spread, The Cheese Thing will be on the table and will be decimated swiftly — my repeat guests have come to expect and crave it. The Cheese Thing defies explanation; what can be said is that it’s very much a personal blog recipe, its name coined by Mitchell Davis and then surfaced more broadly on the internet by Bon Appétit back in 2018. On its surface, it just sounds like a sort of wonky baked ziti. It is the ultimate comfort recipe; cubes of cheese melt into the crevices of penne pasta, melding with a super-simple sweet and buttery tomato sauce. I absolutely shower it in salt, cracked pepper, and fluffy Pecorino, and sometimes bake extra cheese onto the top. I’d consider it a side because it lacks main-course energy and is ideal for a potluck or buffet, but there’s no doubt that it could serve as an entree on a chilly night for two, four, or however many people fit on your couch. — Hilary Pollack, deputy editor.
